2 Part 1: Describing the Centre
When we collect data, the first question is usually: What’s typical?

2.1 The Mean: The Balancing Point
The mean is the arithmetic average. If we measured 5 people’s memory scores:

Please enable JavaScript to experience the dynamic code cell content on this page.
The mean is 7. This is the “balancing point” — if you put these scores on a seesaw, 7 is where it would balance.


2.2 The Median: The Middle Value
The median is the middle value when data are sorted. Half the values are above it, half below.

Please enable JavaScript to experience the dynamic code cell content on this page.
With 5 values, the median is the 3rd value (when sorted). Here, both mean and median are 7.


2.3 When Mean and Median Differ
Sometimes they tell different stories. Consider these scores:

Please enable JavaScript to experience the dynamic code cell content on this page.
The mean shoots up to 10, but the median stays at 7. The median is resistant to extreme values (outliers). The mean is pulled by them.
When to use which?

Mean: When data are roughly symmetric, no extreme outliers
Median: When data are skewed or have outliers (like income data)

title: Chapter 4: Descriptive Statistics in Action
text:
3 Part 2: Describing the Spread
The centre isn’t the whole story. Two groups can have the same mean but look completely different:

Please enable JavaScript to experience the dynamic code cell content on this page.
Both means are 7, but the groups are very different. We need measures of spread.

3.1 The Range: Simplest Spread
The range is just the distance from lowest to highest:

Please enable JavaScript to experience the dynamic code cell content on this page.
Group A spans 2 points (6 to 8). Group B spans 10 points (2 to 12). The range immediately shows Group B is more variable.
Limitation: The range only uses two values, so it’s sensitive to outliers.


3.2 The Standard Deviation: The Gold Standard
The standard deviation (SD) measures how far scores typically fall from the mean.

Please enable JavaScript to experience the dynamic code cell content on this page.
Group A’s SD is about 0.7 — scores cluster tightly around 7. Group B’s SD is about 4.2 — scores are much more spread out.
Rule of thumb: In roughly normal data, about 68% of values fall within 1 SD of the mean.
If the mean is 7 and SD is 1:

~68% of scores fall between 6 and 8



3.3 The summary() Function: Everything at Once
R’s summary() function gives you a quick overview:

Please enable JavaScript to experience the dynamic code cell content on this page.
This shows:

Min and Max (the range endpoints)
1st and 3rd Quartile (the middle 50%)
Median (the middle value)
Mean

title: Chapter 2: DataLab Foundations
text:
2 Reflecting on Data Collection
DataLab was probably your first experience collecting psychological data. You may have noticed things didn’t always go smoothly:

Instructions weren’t always clear
Timing was tricky
Partners did things differently
The environment was distracting
Recording data while running a task was harder than expected

This is normal. In fact, these challenges are exactly why research methods matter. Understanding what can go wrong helps you:

Appreciate why standardised procedures exist
Interpret your own data more thoughtfully
Design better studies in the future

As you read about each task below, think about what happened during your data collection. What might have affected your measurements?

title: Chapter 2: DataLab Foundations
text:
3 What You Measured
DataLab included a group memory test plus five tasks measuring different aspects of human cognition and behaviour. For each task, we’ll cover the psychological background and then consider methodological issues.

3.1 Task 1: Reaction Time (Reflex Test)

Reaction time is the interval between a stimulus and your response to it. In the ruler-drop task, we measured simple reaction time — how quickly you could respond to a single, expected stimulus.
The physics is elegant: when you catch a falling ruler, the distance it fell before you caught it tells us how long your reaction took. Using the equation for free-falling objects (d = ½gt²), we can convert centimetres into milliseconds.






NoteWhy It Matters



Reaction time is one of the most reliable measures in psychology. Your data will show how consistent (or variable) human performance is, even on simple tasks. We can also look for practice effects — did you get faster across trials?








WarningMethodological Considerations



Measurement error:

Was the ruler held at exactly the same height each time?
Did the participant’s fingers start in exactly the same position?
Was it always clear where to read the catch point?

Potential biases:

Anticipation: Did you start to predict when the drop would happen?
Practice effects: Did you genuinely get faster, or just better at anticipating?
Hand dominance: We only tested one hand — would results differ for the other?

Procedural issues:

How consistent was your partner’s dropping technique?
Were there distractions (noise, movement) that affected some trials?
Did everyone follow the same instructions?





3.2 Memory Test: Mind Palace

The memory task measured working memory — how many items you can hold in mind while performing another task.
Miller (1956) famously proposed that we can hold about 7 ± 2 items in short-term memory — the “magical number seven.” But the distraction task (maths problems) interferes with rehearsal, so performance typically drops.
We’ll also examine the serial position effect: people tend to remember words from the beginning of a list (primacy) and end of a list (recency) better than the middle. Your position-by-position recall data will let us test this pattern.






WarningMethodological Considerations



Measurement error:

Were the words presented at the same speed for everyone?
Could everyone hear clearly from where they were sitting?
Was the recall period the same length for all participants?

Potential biases:

Prior exposure: Had you seen any of the words recently?
Language background: Were the words equally familiar to everyone?
Strategy use: Some people use chunking or visualisation — should we control for this?

Procedural issues:

Was the distraction task equally difficult for everyone?
Did the timing between presentation and recall vary?
How was recall scored? (exact spelling? close enough?)





3.3 Task 2: Time and Magnitude Perception (Time Warp)

How accurately do we perceive time? Research shows that our internal clocks are surprisingly inaccurate and can be influenced by many factors.
This station measured three types of estimation:

Time estimation — How accurately could you judge 60 seconds?
Visual magnitude estimation — How accurately could you judge line lengths by looking?
Tactile magnitude estimation — How accurately could you judge lengths by touch alone?







TipCross-Modal Comparison



By comparing visual and tactile estimation, we can explore whether some senses are more accurate than others for judging physical properties.








WarningMethodological Considerations



Measurement error:

When exactly did the stopwatch start? When you said “start” or when your partner pressed it?
How precisely were line lengths measured?
Was string tension consistent across tactile trials?

Potential biases:

Counting: Did you count seconds in your head? (This is a strategy, not pure time perception)
Anchoring: Did early estimates influence later ones?
Expectation: Did you adjust estimates based on feedback?

Procedural issues:

Could you see any clocks or time displays?
Were there environmental cues (regular sounds, movements)?
Was it quiet enough to concentrate?





3.4 Task 3: Psychic Staring (Sixth Sense)

Can humans detect when they’re being watched? This is a testable empirical question!
The staring detection task uses signal detection theory:

Hits: Correctly detecting when someone IS staring
False alarms: Saying “staring” when they’re NOT
Misses: Saying “not staring” when they ARE
Correct rejections: Correctly detecting when they’re NOT staring

If people cannot actually detect staring, we’d expect performance to be at chance level (about 50% correct, or 3 out of 6 trials).






WarningMethodological Considerations



Measurement error:

Could you detect your partner through peripheral vision?
Were there sounds or movements that gave it away?
Was “staring” defined consistently? (How long? How intense?)

Potential biases:

Response bias: Did you tend to say “yes” or “no” more often?
Pattern-seeking: Did you assume alternating patterns?
Confirmation bias: Did you interpret ambiguous feelings as evidence for your guess?

Procedural issues:

How reliably did your partner randomise staring/not-staring?
Was the duration of each trial consistent?
Could other people in the room affect the “being watched” feeling?





3.5 Task 4: Randomness (Lady Luck)

Humans are notoriously bad at generating random sequences. When asked to produce “random” numbers, people:

Avoid repeating the same number twice in a row (even though true randomness includes repetitions)
Avoid patterns (even though random sequences often contain streaks)
Favour certain numbers (often 7!)

This station also included dice rolling and coin flipping, which let us compare true random outcomes (from dice/coins) with human-generated random sequences.






NoteThe Gambler’s Fallacy



Many people believe that after a streak of heads, tails is “due.” This is false — each flip is independent. Your data will likely show longer runs than most people expect!








WarningMethodological Considerations



Measurement error:

Were all 20 numbers recorded correctly?
Were dice rolls and coin flips recorded accurately?
How were “runs” counted? Was this consistent?

Potential biases:

Number preferences: Did cultural factors affect which numbers felt “random”?
Avoidance of repetition: This is a known bias — but did you try to overcome it?
Anchoring: Did your previous number influence your next choice?

Procedural issues:

Was there time pressure that affected your choices?
Did you understand what “random” meant in this context?
Were the dice fair? Were coins flipped properly?





3.6 Task 5: Metacognition (Frontal Lob)

Metacognition is thinking about your own thinking — including how well you know your own abilities.
The throwing task measured calibration: the match between your self-assessed ability and your actual performance.

Overconfidence: Rating yourself higher than your performance
Underconfidence: Rating yourself lower than your performance
Well-calibrated: Your rating matches your performance

Research consistently shows that people are poorly calibrated — often overconfident about easy tasks and underconfident about hard ones.






WarningMethodological Considerations



Measurement error:

How were successful throws defined? What about balls that bounced in?
Who counted the successes — participant or tester?
Was counting accurate across 10 throws?

Potential biases:

Self-serving bias: Did you rate yourself higher because you wanted to be good?
Social desirability: Did having a partner watching affect your self-rating?
Anchoring: Did the 1-10 scale influence what felt like a “reasonable” rating?

Procedural issues:

Was the throwing distance the same for everyone?
Was the target positioned consistently?
Did throwing technique vary (overarm, underarm)?

title: Chapter 2: DataLab Foundations
text:
4 The Pre-Post Design
DataLab used a within-subjects design to measure mood change. You rated your mood, energy, and stress both before and after the stations.
This design is powerful because each person serves as their own control. By comparing your “before” to your “after,” we eliminate individual differences — we’re measuring change within you, not differences between people.






ImportantTeaching Application



When we learn about paired t-tests, we’ll analyse whether DataLab systematically affected mood, energy, or stress. Did participation make people feel better? Worse? More or less stressed?

title: Chapter 2: DataLab Foundations
text:
5 Why This Matters
You’ve just experienced something important: collecting data is hard.
The methodological issues above aren’t criticisms — they’re reality. Even professional researchers face these challenges. The difference is that professionals:

Use standardised procedures — detailed protocols that specify exactly how to do each step
Define variables operationally — clear definitions of what counts as a “catch” or a “success”
Train testers — so everyone administers tasks the same way
Control the environment — quiet rooms, consistent setups, minimal distractions
Check inter-rater reliability — do two testers recording the same event get the same result?

When we analyse your DataLab data, we’ll need to keep these limitations in mind. Some variability in the data reflects genuine individual differences. Some reflects measurement error and procedural inconsistencies.
Learning to tell the difference is what research methods is all about.

6.1 Learning with Real Data

6.2 Experiencing Both Roles
Acting as both participant and tester taught you:

How instructions affect behaviour
Why research protocols exist



6.3 Understanding Limitations
Having collected data yourself, you now understand:

Why researchers obsess over procedures
How small variations can affect results
That “messy data” is normal — interpretation requires care

Concrete words will be easier to rememberAbstract words will be easier to rememberThere will be no difference in recall between word typesMemory is always the same
Q3.7 Why might concrete words be easier to remember?






TipThe Answer: Dual Coding Theory





Concrete words can be stored in TWO ways: as a verbal code (the word) AND as a visual image (you can picture “chair”). Abstract words only have the verbal code. Two codes = better memory.

title: Design Detectives: DataLab

Task 5: Sleep & Memory

The Question
Before the session, you told us how many hours you slept last night. We also measured how many words you recalled.
Is there a relationship between sleep and memory?


Your Results











Group Discussion Questions
Q5.1 Is there an IV in this study?
Yes - sleep hoursYes - memory scoreNo - we measured both variables, we didn’t manipulate eitherYes - the participant
Q5.2 What design type is this? (See correlational design)
Between-subjectsWithin-subjectsCorrelationalExperimental
Q5.3 What does a positive correlation mean here?
Sleep causes better memoryPeople who slept more tended to recall more wordsPeople who slept less recalled more wordsThere is no relationship
Q5.4 Can we say that sleep causes better memory based on this data?
TRUEFALSE
Q5.5 Why can’t we make causal claims from correlational data?
The sample was too smallThe correlation wasn’t strong enoughThird variables might explain the relationship (e.g., health, motivation)Correlations are always meaningless






WarningThe Critical Point: Correlation ≠ Causation



Even if we find a relationship between sleep and memory, we cannot say sleep causes better memory. Why?

Maybe healthier people sleep more AND have better memory
Maybe motivated students prepare better (sleep AND study)
Maybe stress reduces both sleep AND memory

This is why experiments (with manipulation) are needed to establish causation.

What You Did
6 trials: Someone either stared at you or didn’t. You guessed which.
If just guessing randomly: You’d expect to get 3 out of 6 correct (50%).


Your Results











Group Discussion Questions
Q6.1 If someone got 5 out of 6 correct, does that prove they have a sixth sense?
TRUEFALSE
Q6.2 Why not?
5/6 is impossibleSome people will get 5/6 just by luck, even without any real abilityThe experiment was designed wrongSixth sense definitely doesn’t exist
Q6.3 What does 50% accuracy suggest?
They definitely have a sixth senseThey definitely don’t have a sixth sensePerformance is at chance level - consistent with random guessingThe task was too hard
Q6.4 What is the null hypothesis for this study?
People can detect staringPeople cannot detect staringDetection accuracy equals 50% (chance level)There is no null hypothesis






TipWhy Statistics Matter





With 28 people, some will get lucky just by chance. If everyone flipped a coin 6 times, someone would get 5 or 6 heads - but that doesn’t mean their coin is biased!
Statistics help us ask: Is this result more extreme than we’d expect from chance alone?

title: Week 12 Preview Video

Key Concepts Preview

The Big Question
How do we go from raw data to meaningful summaries?
When you collected reaction times in DataLab, you generated dozens of individual measurements. This week, we learn how to compress that information into statistics that tell a clear story.


Central Tendency
Where is the “centre” of the data?

Mean: The arithmetic average — add everything up, divide by how many
Median: The middle value when sorted — resistant to outliers
Mode: The most common value — useful for categories



Variability
How spread out is the data?

Range: Maximum minus minimum — simple but limited
Standard deviation: How far, on average, values are from the mean



Distribution Shape
What does the data look like?

Normal: Symmetric, bell-shaped
Skewed: Tail on one side (positive = right, negative = left)
Bimodal: Two peaks

What Is This Module?
Research Methods & Experimental Design
How psychologists:

Ask questions about the mind and behaviour
Design studies to answer those questions
Collect and analyse data

Emphasise this is a practical, skills-based module. Not just theory — they will DO research.

title: Your Data, Your Discoveries
text:
The Problem with Common Sense

“Opposites attract”
“Birds of a feather flock together”
Both can’t be true… can they?



Common sense often gives contradictory answers. Science provides a systematic way to find out what’s actually true.

title: Your Data, Your Discoveries
text:
Everyday Thinking vs Scientific Thinking


Everyday Thinking

Based on personal experience
Influenced by biases
Accepts anecdotes as evidence
Confirmation bias
“I just know”


Scientific Thinking

Based on systematic observation
Controls for biases
Requires replicable evidence
Seeks disconfirmation
“Let’s test it”

Transferable skills for any career

From Question to Knowledge





flowchart LR
    Q[Research Question] --> H[Hypothesis]
    H --> D[Design Study]

title: Your Data, Your Discoveries
text:
Step 1: The Research Question
Where do research questions come from?

Curiosity about behaviour
Gaps in existing research
Real-world problems
Theory testing
Unexpected observations


Example: Do people lie more when texting than face-to-face?

title: Your Data, Your Discoveries
text:
Step 2: The Hypothesis

A hypothesis is a specific, testable prediction about what you expect to find.

Good hypothesis:

“Participants will tell more lies per conversation when communicating via text message compared to face-to-face.”

Not a hypothesis:

“I wonder if texting affects lying.”

title: Your Data, Your Discoveries
text:
Step 3: Design the Study
Key decisions:

Who will you study? (participants)
What will you measure? (variables)
How will you measure it? (methods)
What comparisons will you make? (design)


We’ll spend most of this module on this step.

title: Your Data, Your Discoveries
text:
Step 4: Collect Data

Follow your plan precisely
Treat participants ethically
Record everything carefully
Minimise errors and bias

title: Your Data, Your Discoveries
text:
Step 5: Analyse Data

Statistics are tools for finding patterns in data and determining whether those patterns are meaningful.

This is where R comes in — and what you’ll learn in the labs.

title: Your Data, Your Discoveries
text:
Step 6: Interpret Results

What do the findings mean?
Do they support the hypothesis?
What are the limitations?
What questions remain?


Then the cycle continues…

Writing a Hypothesis

Experimental hypothesis (H₁): Predicts an effect or difference
Null hypothesis (H₀): Predicts no effect or no difference


For the memory experiment:

H₁: Concrete words will be easier to remember than abstract words

title: Your Data, Your Discoveries
text:
One-Tailed vs Two-Tailed

One-tailed: Predicts the direction of the effect
Two-tailed: Predicts a difference but not which direction

title: Your Data, Your Discoveries

This Is Within-Subjects Design

Within-subjects design: The same participants measured in all conditions



Pre-mood and post-mood came from the same person
You’re being compared to yourself

title: Your Data, Your Discoveries
text:
Why Is This Powerful?






The Power of Within-Subjects


Each person is their own control!




Individual differences are controlled:

If your pre-mood was 5 and post-mood was 7…
You improved by 2 points
We don’t need to worry about other people’s baseline moods

title: Your Data, Your Discoveries
text:
Self-Rating vs Actual Performance
Before the throwing task, you rated how good you thought you’d be.
Question: Do people know themselves?

title: Your Data, Your Discoveries
text:
This Is Correlational Design

Correlational design: Measuring the relationship between two variables — no manipulation



Variable 1: Self-rating (1-10)
Variable 2: Actual accuracy (%)









Key Point


There is no IV in a correlational design!

title: Your Data, Your Discoveries
text:
The Critical Warning






Say It With Me


Correlation ≠ Causation
Finding a relationship does NOT mean one variable causes the other.




Even if self-ratings predict performance, we can’t say self-ratings cause good performance.

Does getting 5 or 6 right mean you have a sixth sense?




Not necessarily!


If you flip a coin 6 times, sometimes you get 5 or 6 heads just by luck.

title: Your Data, Your Discoveries
text:
The Null Hypothesis

Null hypothesis (H₀): The result is due to chance, not a real effect.


For the sixth sense:

H₀: People are just guessing (performance = 50%)
H₁: People can detect staring (performance ≠ 50%)

title: DataLab: Grow Your Own Psychology Data
text:
Task 1: Reflex Test





How fast is your nervous system?
Measure your reaction time using a ruler-drop task.

What You’ll Do

Partner A holds the ruler at the 30cm mark, letting it hang vertically
Partner B positions thumb and finger at the 0cm mark — don’t touch!
Partner A drops the ruler without warning (within 5 seconds)
Partner B catches it as fast as possible
Read the cm mark at the top of your thumb
Complete 5 trials, then swap roles



What You’ll Record

Which hand you used (dominant or non-dominant)
The distance caught on each trial (in cm)
Any trials you missed

title: DataLab: Grow Your Own Psychology Data
text:
Task 2: Time Warp





Your brain’s internal clock
Explore how accurately you perceive time and physical dimensions.

Part A: 60-Second Estimation

Close your eyes
When you hear “Start”, sense time passing
Say “Stop” when you think 60 seconds have passed
Record the actual time



Part B: Visual Estimation (Lines)

Look at Line Card A — estimate its length in cm
Repeat with Line Card B



Part C: Tactile Estimation (Strings)

Feel String 1 with eyes closed — estimate its length in cm
Repeat with String 2



What You’ll Record

Your 60-second estimate (actual seconds)
Line estimates (cm)
String estimates (cm)
Whether you counted

title: DataLab: Grow Your Own Psychology Data
text:
Task 3: Sixth Sense





Can you tell when someone is watching you?

What You’ll Do

Sit back-to-back with your partner (~1m apart)
STARER: Flip the coin

Heads = Stare at partner’s head
Tails = Look away

Hold for 15 seconds
TARGET: Say “Staring” or “Not staring”
Rate your confidence (1 = guess, 5 = certain)
Complete 6 trials as target, then swap



What You’ll Record

For each trial: actual, guess, confidence
Total correct out of 6

title: DataLab: Grow Your Own Psychology Data
text:
Task 4: Lady Luck





How random can you be?

Part A: Random Numbers
Say 20 “random” numbers between 1 and 10 aloud. Partner records them.


Part B: Dice Rolling

Predict: more 6s than expected by chance?
Roll the die 10 times, record each



Part C: Coin Flipping

Flip 10 times, record each (H or T)
Note the longest run



What You’ll Record

All 20 numbers
Dice prediction and outcomes
Coin outcomes and longest run

title: DataLab: Grow Your Own Psychology Data
text:
Task 5: Frontal Lob





Precision meets confidence

What You’ll Do

Before throwing: Rate your throwing ability (1–10)
Stand at the marked line
Throw 10 ping pong balls at the basket
Count your successes



What You’ll Record

Your self-rating (1–10)
Number of successes (out of 10)
Which is your dominant hand

How you’re feeling now (compare to before)

By measuring your mood before AND after, we can see if DataLab affected how you feel. This is a within-subjects design.

title: Chapter 1: Introduction to Research Methods
text:
TipBefore You Begin



This is your first reading for PS50008A. Take your time with it. The concepts introduced here form the foundation for everything else in this module.




You chose psychology because you want to understand people. Why do we remember some things and forget others? What drives someone to help a stranger—or to hurt them? How do our early experiences shape who we become? These questions drew you here, and they’re genuinely worth exploring.
Then you look at your timetable and see “Research Methods and Experimental Design.”
If your heart sinks a little, you’re not alone - but I’m going to try to turn this around. This material has a reputation, and not a glamorous one. But there are real reasons it’s central to your degree—not because we enjoy watching you suffer, but because it changes what you’re capable of doing. It’s powerful stuff!

text:
TipBefore You Begin



This is your first reading for PS50008A. Take your time with it. The concepts introduced here form the foundation for everything else in this module.




You chose psychology because you want to understand people. Why do we remember some things and forget others? What drives someone to help a stranger—or to hurt them? How do our early experiences shape who we become? These questions drew you here, and they’re genuinely worth exploring.
Then you look at your timetable and see “Research Methods and Experimental Design.”
If your heart sinks a little, you’re not alone - but I’m going to try to turn this around. This material has a reputation, and not a glamorous one. But there are real reasons it’s central to your degree—not because we enjoy watching you suffer, but because it changes what you’re capable of doing. It’s powerful stuff!

title: Chapter 1: Introduction to Research Methods
section: You’re Learning to Ask Questions Properly
text:
You’re Learning to Ask Questions Properly
Right now, if someone asked you “Does social media cause anxiety?”, you might have an opinion. Everyone has one of those. But psychology isn’t about opinions—it’s about evidence. And evidence doesn’t just land in your lap. Someone has to design a way to gather it, collect it carefully, and work out what it actually shows.
That’s what you’re learning to do. By the end of your degree, you won’t just think social media might cause anxiety—you’ll be able to design a study that could actually test the idea, spot the weaknesses in existing research, and understand why the answer might be more complicated than the headlines suggest.

Think about that for a second… You don’t have to rely on anecdote or opinion anymore. You can create knowledge.

title: Chapter 1: Introduction to Research Methods
text:
You’ll See Through the Nonsense
We’re surrounded by claims about human behaviour. Adverts tell us certain products will make us more confident. Influencers promote supplements that supposedly sharpen your mind. News stories announce that scientists have “proved” all sorts of things about personality, intelligence, or relationships. 9 out of 10 adverts are dubious! (not a real stat!)
Most of these claims are, at best, oversimplified. Many are outright wrong. Understanding research methods gives you the ability to look at a study and ask:

How many people did they actually test?
Could something else explain these results?
Is this finding likely to replicate?

This isn’t just academic scepticism. It’s protection against being manipulated by people who use the language of science without the rigour, without the appropriate ‘methods’.

title: Chapter 1: Introduction to Research Methods
text:
These Skills Travel
Psychology graduates end up in all sorts of places: clinical training, education, marketing, human resources, policy research, user experience design, data analysis, all sorts of entrepreneurial activities I don’t understand. What connects these fields is that they all involve understanding people and making decisions based on evidence. It’s just thinking scientifically.
The ability to gather data systematically, analyse it honestly, and communicate what it means is valuable almost everywhere. It’s also incredibly rare. Many people can express opinions confidently; fewer can actually interrogate those opinions with evidence.

title: Chapter 1: Introduction to Research Methods
text:
And One More Thing
Some of you will genuinely enjoy this. Not everyone, and probably not immediately, but there’s real satisfaction in solving methodological puzzles: working out how to test something that seems untestable, spotting a flaw in an argument, seeing a pattern emerge from data you collected yourself.
I’m not promising you’ll love every moment. But we are promising that this material is worth taking seriously—and that taking it seriously might surprise you.






ImportantThis Week



Since Week 11 has no lecture, use this reading to prepare for the term ahead. But above all, be curious!








Note



Sophie von Stumm (formerly from Goldsmiths!) and colleagues (2011) sought to identify the best predictors of academic performance. Unsurprisingly perhaps, a person’s intelligence was the best predictor. However, they also found that this was matched by the combined predictive power of effort and intellectual curiosity. They conclude that succeeding in academic fields (such as psychology) is not just a question of being smart and trying hard, it is also about having a hungry mind!

Von Stumm, S., Hell, B., & Chamorro-Premuzic, T. (2011). The hungry mind: Intellectual curiosity is the third pillar of academic performance. Perspectives on Psychological Science, 6, 574-588.

title: Chapter 1: Introduction to Research Methods
text:
Why Do Psychologists Do Research?
Psychology aims to understand human behaviour and mental processes. But how do we move from casual observation to scientific knowledge?

The Problem with Common Sense
We often think we understand human behaviour based on everyday experience - my mum certainly thinks so. But “common sense” has limitations (sorry, mum!):

Hindsight bias: Events seem obvious after they occur (“I knew it all along”)
Confirmation bias: We notice evidence that supports our beliefs and ignore contradicting evidence
Anecdotal evidence: Individual cases can mislead — your friend’s experience isn’t representative of everyone

Consider these “common sense” claims:

“Opposites attract” — But also “Birds of a feather flock together”
“Too many cooks spoil the broth” — But also “Many hands make light work”
“Absence makes the heart grow fonder” — But also “Out of sight, out of mind”

Common sense can justify almost any conclusion. Research methods provide systematic tools to overcome these biases and determine which claims actually hold up under scrutiny.


Why Intuitions About Behaviour Are Often Wrong
Our intuitions fail us for several reasons:

We don’t see our own blind spots — We’re unaware of the biases affecting our judgement
Memory is reconstructive — We misremember events to fit our current beliefs
We overgeneralise from small samples — One or two examples feel like proof
We confuse correlation with causation — Two things happening together doesn’t mean one caused the other

For example, studies consistently show that:

People are poor at predicting what will make them happy
Eyewitness testimony is far less reliable than we assume
“Venting” anger often increases rather than decreases aggression

These findings contradict common intuitions — which is precisely why we need systematic research.

title: Chapter 1: Introduction to Research Methods
text:
What Makes a Claim Scientific?

The Difference Between Opinion and Science
An opinion is a personal belief that may or may not be supported by evidence: > “I think social media makes people unhappy.”
A scientific claim is testable, based on systematic evidence, and open to being proven wrong: > “In a study of 1,000 adults, those who used social media for more than 3 hours daily reported lower life satisfaction scores (M = 5.2) than those who used it less than 1 hour (M = 6.8), t(998) = 4.32, p < .001.”


Four Hallmarks of Scientific Claims


Empirical basis — Based on observable, measurable evidence, not just reasoning or authority
Systematic collection — Data gathered using consistent, documented methods
Falsifiability — The claim could, in principle, be proven wrong by evidence
Transparency — Methods are described clearly enough that others could repeat them




What “Replicable” Means
A finding is replicable if other researchers, following the same procedures, get the same results.
Why does this matter?

A single study might have flaws we don’t notice
Random chance can produce misleading results
Researcher bias might influence findings

When multiple independent teams find the same result, we can be more confident it’s real.






NoteThe Replication Crisis



Psychology has faced a “replication crisis” — many classic findings failed to replicate when researchers tried to repeat them. This has led to better practices: larger samples, pre-registration of hypotheses, and more transparency. You’ll learn about this in Week 17.

title: Chapter 1: Introduction to Research Methods
text:
The Scientific Method
Researchers typically follow these steps:

1. Identify a Question
Start with curiosity. What do you want to understand?

“Do people remember information better if they test themselves rather than just re-reading?”



2. Review Existing Knowledge
What have others already discovered? Build on previous work rather than starting from scratch.


3. Formulate a Hypothesis
Make a specific, testable prediction.

“Students who use self-testing will recall more information after one week than students who re-read the material.”



4. Design a Study
Plan exactly how you’ll test your hypothesis: - Who will you study? - What will you measure? - How will you control for other explanations?


5. Collect Data
Gather observations systematically, following your planned procedures.


6. Analyse Results
Use statistics to determine whether your findings are meaningful or could have occurred by chance.


7. Draw Conclusions
What do your results mean? Do they support your hypothesis? What are the limitations?


8. Report Findings
Share your methods and results so others can evaluate and build on your work.
You’ll work through all these steps in your group project this term.

title: Chapter 1: Introduction to Research Methods
text:
Variables: Things That Vary
A variable is anything that can take different values.

Examples of Variables



Variable
Possible Values




Height
150cm, 165cm, 180cm…


Reaction time
200ms, 350ms, 420ms…


Mood
Happy, sad, anxious, neutral…


Number of words recalled
0, 1, 2, 3… 20


Exam score
0-100





Why Variables Matter
Research is fundamentally about understanding how variables relate to each other:

Does study time affect exam performance?
Does sleep quality predict reaction time?
Is age related to memory capacity?

In DataLab, you’ll measure several variables and see how they differ between people and across conditions.


Types of Variables
Continuous variables can take any value within a range: - Height (175.3cm) - Reaction time (287.4ms) - Temperature (36.8°C)
Categorical variables fall into distinct categories: - Gender (male, female, non-binary) - Experimental condition (control, treatment) - Handedness (left, right, ambidextrous)
Discrete variables are countable whole numbers: - Number of items recalled (7) - Number of errors (3) - Number of children (2)
Understanding variable types helps you choose appropriate statistical analyses — something you’ll learn throughout this module.

title: Chapter 1: Introduction to Research Methods
section: How Empirical Evidence Helps Us Understand Behaviour
text:
How Empirical Evidence Helps Us Understand Behaviour

Moving Beyond Speculation
Without data, debates about human behaviour often go in circles. Everyone has opinions, but how do we know whose is correct?
Empirical evidence allows us to:

Test competing theories — Instead of arguing, we can design studies to see which prediction holds
Discover unexpected findings — Data often reveals patterns we wouldn’t have predicted
Quantify effects — Not just “X affects Y” but “X increases Y by approximately this much”
Identify boundary conditions — Under what circumstances does a finding hold or not hold?



An Example: Does Punishment Deter Crime?
Common sense might suggest that harsher punishments reduce crime. But what does the evidence show?
Research has found: - Certainty of punishment matters more than severity - Very harsh sentences may actually increase recidivism in some cases - Deterrent effects vary by crime type and offender characteristics
Without systematic data collection, we’d have no way to discover these nuances.

title: Chapter 1: Introduction to Research Methods
text:
Connecting to DataLab

Your Data, Your Learning
In Thursday’s lab, you’ll experience research from both perspectives:

As a participant — completing cognitive tasks
As a tester — administering tasks and recording data

This dual perspective helps you understand:

Why standardised procedures matter (you’ll see what happens when instructions vary)
How measurement introduces variability (the same person gives different responses across trials)
What it feels like to generate data that will be analysed

The data you generate will be used throughout the term. When we discuss distributions in Week 12, we’ll look at the distribution of YOUR reaction times. When we learn about t-tests in Week 14, we’ll compare performance between Room A and Room B. This is your data, and you’ll learn statistics by exploring it.

title: Station 4: Sixth Sense
text:
Station Overview
The Sixth Sense station tests whether people can detect when someone is staring at them from behind. This classic psychology experiment creates a signal detection paradigm where we can calculate hit rates, false alarm rates, and test performance against chance (50%). Spoiler: most research finds no evidence for “gaze detection” beyond chance!

title: Station 4: Sixth Sense
text:
What Participants Do

Sit back-to-back with your partner (~1m apart)
STARER: Flip a coin

Heads = Stare intently at partner’s head
Tails = Look away (at the floor or wall)

Hold for 15 seconds
TARGET: Say “Staring” or “Not staring”
Rate your confidence (1 = guessing, 5 = certain)
Complete 6 trials as target, then swap roles

title: Station 4: Sixth Sense
text:
Research Questions

Can people detect when they are being stared at better than chance (50%)?


Is confidence related to accuracy?


Do believers in psychic phenomena perform differently?

title: Station 4: Sixth Sense
text:
Experimental Design



Element
Description




Design
Signal detection paradigm


Signal
Partner staring (coin = Heads)


Noise
Partner not staring (coin = Tails)


Response
“Staring” or “Not staring”


Measure
Accuracy, confidence, hit rate, false alarm rate

title: Station 4: Sixth Sense
text:
Signal Detection Theory



Outcome
Actual: Staring
Actual: Not Staring




Guess: Staring
Hit ✓
False Alarm


Guess: Not Staring
Miss
Correct Rejection ✓









NoteTesting Against Chance



With 6 trials and 50% chance, we expect participants to get 3 correct by guessing randomly. We use a one-sample t-test to compare the group mean to 3 (or equivalently, test if proportion correct differs from 0.5).

title: Station 4: Sixth Sense
text:
Expected Results



Metric
Expected Value




Mean correct
~3 out of 6 (50%)


Hit rate
~0.5


False alarm rate
~0.5


Confidence
Often higher than accuracy warrants









WarningThe Null Hypothesis



The null hypothesis for this task is that people cannot detect gaze better than chance. Published research consistently fails to reject this null — there’s no reliable evidence for “sixth sense” gaze detection!

title: Station 4: Sixth Sense
text:
Suggested Analyses
Primary analysis:

One-sample t-test: Is mean correct different from 3?
Alternatively: Binomial test against 50%

Signal detection analysis:

Calculate hit rate and false alarm rate
Compare d’ (sensitivity) across conditions

Exploratory analyses:

Correlation between confidence and accuracy
Compare believers vs sceptics

title: Station 4: Sixth Sense
text:
R Code Starter
# Load data
datalab <- read_csv("datalab_data.csv")

# Calculate correct total (need to create from individual trials)
# Assuming trial data is in separate columns

# One-sample t-test: Is mean different from chance (3)?
t.test(datalab$stare_correct_total, mu = 3)

# Descriptive statistics
datalab |>
  summarise(
    mean_correct = mean(stare_correct_total, na.rm = TRUE),
    sd_correct = sd(stare_correct_total, na.rm = TRUE),
    prop_above_chance = mean(stare_correct_total > 3, na.rm = TRUE)
  )

# Hit rate and false alarm rate (per participant)
# Would need trial-level data manipulation

# Visualise distribution
library(ggplot2)
ggplot(datalab, aes(x = stare_correct_total)) +
  geom_histogram(binwidth = 1, fill = "#275882", colour = "white") +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 3, colour = "#EA8439", linewidth = 1.5, linetype = "dashed") +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = 0:6) +
  labs(
    x = "Number Correct (out of 6)",
    y = "Count",
    title = "Sixth Sense Performance",
    subtitle = "Dashed line = chance performance (3/6)"
  )

title: Station 4: Sixth Sense
text:
Tips for Facilitators

Partners should sit truly back-to-back — no peeking!
The starer must commit fully to staring OR looking away
Coin flips should be hidden from the target
Confidence ratings are valuable — encourage honest self-assessment
If working solo, participants can use an online random generator

title: Station 2: Mind Palace
text:
Station Overview
The Mind Palace station tests short-term memory using a classic word list paradigm. Participants study a list of 10 words, complete a distractor task, then recall as many words as possible. This station demonstrates the serial position effect — the tendency to remember words at the beginning (primacy) and end (recency) of a list better than those in the middle.
Additionally, this station implements a between-groups manipulation: Lab 304A sees abstract words with background music, while Lab 304B sees concrete words in silence.

title: Station 2: Mind Palace
text:
What Participants Do

STUDY (30 seconds): Memorise 10 words shown on screen
DISTRACT (60 seconds): Complete simple maths problems
RECALL (90 seconds): Write down as many words as remembered on paper
RECORD: Enter results in Qualtrics — total recalled, which positions, intrusions

title: Station 2: Mind Palace
text:
Research Questions

Do participants recall more words from the beginning and end of the list (serial position effect)?


Do concrete words lead to better recall than abstract words (between-labs comparison)?


Does background music affect memory performance?

title: Station 2: Mind Palace
text:
R Code Starter
# Load data
datalab <- read_csv("datalab_data.csv")

# Compare total recall between labs
datalab |>
  group_by(lab_room) |>
  summarise(
    mean_recall = mean(mem_total, na.rm = TRUE),
    sd_recall = sd(mem_total, na.rm = TRUE),
    n = n()
  )

# Independent t-test
t.test(mem_total ~ lab_room, data = datalab)

# Serial position analysis
library(tidyr)
library(ggplot2)

# Convert position data to long format
position_data <- datalab |>
  select(participant_id, lab_room, mem_pos1:mem_pos10) |>
  pivot_longer(
    cols = starts_with("mem_pos"),
    names_to = "position",
    values_to = "recalled"
  ) |>
  mutate(
    position = parse_number(position),
    recalled = if_else(recalled == "Yes", 1, 0)
  )

# Calculate proportion recalled at each position
serial_curve <- position_data |>
  group_by(position) |>
  summarise(prop_recalled = mean(recalled, na.rm = TRUE))

# Plot serial position curve
ggplot(serial_curve, aes(x = position, y = prop_recalled)) +
  geom_line(colour = "#275882", linewidth = 1.2) +
  geom_point(colour = "#EA8439", size = 3) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = 1:10) +
  scale_y_continuous(limits = c(0, 1), labels = scales::percent) +
  labs(
    x = "Serial Position",
    y = "Proportion Recalled",
    title = "Serial Position Curve"
  )

title: Station 2: Mind Palace
text:
Tips for Facilitators

This station is completed together as a whole-lab activity
Ensure participants only look at their assigned list (left or right side of screen)
The 60-second distractor task is crucial — it clears short-term memory
Remind participants to write on paper during recall, not look back at the screen
Intrusions (false memories) are valuable data — encourage honest reporting

title: Station 6: Frontal Lob
text:
Station Overview
The Frontal Lob station investigates metacognition — your ability to accurately predict your own performance. Before throwing ping pong balls at a target, participants rate their throwing ability. We then compare their self-rating to actual performance, calculating a calibration score that reveals whether people are overconfident, underconfident, or well-calibrated.

title: Station 6: Frontal Lob
text:
What Participants Do

Before throwing: Rate your throwing ability (1–10)
Stand at the marked line
Throw 10 ping pong balls at the basket (dominant hand)
Optionally: Throw 5 more with your non-dominant hand
Count your successes

title: Station 6: Frontal Lob
text:
Research Questions

Is self-rated ability correlated with actual performance?


Are people generally overconfident or underconfident?


Does dominant vs non-dominant hand performance differ?

Element
Description

Measure
Calibration = accuracy − rating

ImportantCalibration Score Interpretation




Positive calibration: Performed better than predicted → underconfident
Negative calibration: Predicted better than performed → overconfident
Zero calibration: Perfect self-knowledge!

title: Station 6: Frontal Lob

Expected Results







Metric
Typical Finding




Mean success rate
~40–60% (4–6 out of 10)


Self-rating mean
Often slightly higher than actual


Calibration
Slight overconfidence (negative mean)


Correlation (rating vs performance)
Moderate positive (r ≈ 0.3–0.5)









NoteThe Dunning-Kruger Effect?



This task can reveal calibration biases. Research on metacognition shows that people are often poorly calibrated — we think we’re better at things than we actually are. However, the relationship is complex and depends on task difficulty and expertise.

title: Station 6: Frontal Lob
text:
Suggested Analyses
Primary analyses:

Pearson’s r: Correlation between self-rating and success
Scatterplot: Visualise the relationship

Calibration analysis:

Calculate mean calibration score
One-sample t-test: Is mean calibration different from 0?

Exploratory analyses:

Compare dominant vs non-dominant hand performance
Correlate conscientiousness (TIPI) with calibration

title: Station 6: Frontal Lob
text:
R Code Starter
# Load data
datalab <- read_csv("datalab_data.csv")

# Calculate calibration
datalab <- datalab |>
  mutate(
    throw_accuracy_pct = (throw_dom_success / 10) * 100,
    throw_calibration = (throw_accuracy_pct / 10) - throw_self_rating
  )

# Correlation between self-rating and performance
cor.test(datalab$throw_self_rating, datalab$throw_dom_success)

# Mean calibration (are people overconfident?)
datalab |>
  summarise(
    mean_calibration = mean(throw_calibration, na.rm = TRUE),
    sd_calibration = sd(throw_calibration, na.rm = TRUE)
  )

# One-sample t-test: Is calibration different from 0?
t.test(datalab$throw_calibration, mu = 0)

# Scatterplot
library(ggplot2)
ggplot(datalab, aes(x = throw_self_rating, y = throw_dom_success)) +
  geom_jitter(width = 0.2, height = 0.2, alpha = 0.6, colour = "#275882") +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", se = TRUE, colour = "#EA8439") +
  geom_abline(slope = 1, intercept = 0, linetype = "dashed", colour = "grey50") +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = 1:10) +
  scale_y_continuous(breaks = 0:10) +
  labs(
    x = "Self-Rated Ability (1-10)",
    y = "Actual Success (out of 10)",
    title = "Self-Prediction vs Actual Performance",
    subtitle = "Dashed line = perfect calibration"
  ) +
  coord_fixed()

title: Spearman’s rho
text: Spearman’s rho (ρ or rs) is a non-parametric correlation coefficient that measures the strength and direction of the monotonic relationship between two variables using ranked data.

title: Spearman’s rho
text: Spearman’s rho (ρ or rs) is a non-parametric correlation coefficient that measures the strength and direction of the monotonic relationship between two variables using ranked data.

title: Spearman’s rho
text:
When to Use
Use Spearman’s rho when:

Data are ordinal (ranked)
Relationship is monotonic (but not necessarily linear)
Assumptions of Pearson’s r are violated
Outliers are present
Data are not normally distributed

title: Spearman’s rho
text:
How It Works

Rank both variables separately
Calculate Pearson’s r on the ranks
Result: Spearman’s rho

title: Spearman’s rho
text:
The Formula
\[\rho = 1 - \frac{6\sum d_i^2}{n(n^2-1)}\]
Where d = difference between ranks for each pair.

title: Paired t-test
text: A paired t-test (also called dependent or related-samples t-test) compares two means that come from the same participants or matched pairs. It tests whether the average difference between paired observations is significantly different from zero.

title: Paired t-test
text: A paired t-test (also called dependent or related-samples t-test) compares two means that come from the same participants or matched pairs. It tests whether the average difference between paired observations is significantly different from zero.

title: Paired t-test
text:
When to Use
Use a paired t-test when:

Same participants measured twice (e.g., before/after)
Participants matched in pairs across conditions
Comparing two conditions in a within-groups design
Data are approximately normally distributed (or n > 30)

title: Paired t-test
text:
The Formula
\[t = \frac{\bar{d}}{s_d / \sqrt{n}}\]
Where:

\(\bar{d}\) = mean of the differences
\(s_d\) = standard deviation of the differences
\(n\) = number of pairs

title: Paired t-test
text:
Assumptions



Assumption
Check




Paired observations
Each participant provides two scores


Independence
Different pairs are independent


Normal differences
Difference scores approximately normal


Continuous data
Interval or ratio scale

title: Paired t-test
text:
Effect Size
Calculate Cohen’s d for paired data:
\[d = \frac{\bar{d}}{s_d}\]



d value
Interpretation




0.2
Small effect


0.5
Medium effect


0.8
Large effect

title: Paired t-test
text:
R Code Example
# Paired t-test
t.test(condition_a, condition_b, paired = TRUE)

# Or with difference scores
differences <- condition_a - condition_b
t.test(differences, mu = 0)

# Effect size
library(effectsize)
cohens_d(condition_a, condition_b, paired = TRUE)

text:

A paired-samples t-test revealed a significant difference between Condition A (M = 450, SD = 52) and Condition B (M = 425, SD = 48), t(29) = 3.45, p = .002, d = 0.63.

title: Independent t-test
text: An independent t-test (also called unpaired or two-sample t-test) compares the means of two separate groups of participants. It tests whether the difference between group means is significantly different from zero.

title: Independent t-test
text: An independent t-test (also called unpaired or two-sample t-test) compares the means of two separate groups of participants. It tests whether the difference between group means is significantly different from zero.

title: Independent t-test
text:
When to Use
Use an independent t-test when:

Comparing two different groups of participants
Groups are independent (no participant in both groups)
Testing a between-groups design
Data are approximately normally distributed (or n > 30 per group)

title: Independent t-test
text:
The Formula
\[t = \frac{\bar{X}_1 - \bar{X}_2}{SE_{pooled}}\]
Where the pooled standard error depends on whether variances are assumed equal.

title: Independent t-test
text:
Assumptions



Assumption
Check




Independence

Normality

Homogeneity of variance
Similar spread in both groups


Continuous data
Interval or ratio scale

title: Independent t-test
text:
Welch’s t-test
When variances are unequal, use Welch’s t-test (the default in R):

Does not assume equal variances
Adjusts degrees of freedom
More robust in most situations

title: Independent t-test
text:
Effect Size
Calculate Cohen’s d:
\[d = \frac{\bar{X}_1 - \bar{X}_2}{s_{pooled}}\]



d value
Interpretation




0.2
Small effect


0.5
Medium effect


0.8
Large effect

text:
R Code Example

t.test(score ~ group, data = mydata)

# Student's t-test (assumes equal variance)
t.test(score ~ group, data = mydata, var.equal = TRUE)

# Effect size
library(effectsize)
cohens_d(score ~ group, data = mydata)

text:

An independent-samples t-test showed that Group A (M = 72.3, SD = 8.4) scored significantly higher than Group B (M = 65.1, SD = 9.2), t(58) = 3.21, p = .002, d = 0.82.

Parametric Assumptions
Use parametric tests when:

title: Within-Groups Design
text: A within-groups design (also called within-subjects or repeated-measures design) is an experimental approach where the same participants are tested under all conditions of the independent variable.

title: Within-Groups Design
text: A within-groups design (also called within-subjects or repeated-measures design) is an experimental approach where the same participants are tested under all conditions of the independent variable.

title: Within-Groups Design
text:
Key Characteristics



Feature
Description




Participants
Same individuals in all conditions


Comparison
Each person serves as their own control


Sample size
Typically requires fewer participants


Control
Individual differences eliminated

title: Within-Groups Design
text:
Advantages

Eliminates individual differences: Each participant acts as their own control, removing between-person variability
Statistical power: Requires fewer participants to detect effects
Efficiency: Collects more data per participant

title: Within-Groups Design
text:
Disadvantages

Order effects: Performance may change due to practice, fatigue, or carryover
Demand characteristics: Participants may guess the hypothesis
Time constraints: Sessions may be longer

title: Within-Groups Design
text:
Example
Testing whether people respond faster to images or words:

Condition A: Participant responds to 50 images
Condition B: Same participant responds to 50 words
Comparison: Response times compared within each individual

title: Within-Groups Design
text:
Controlling for Order Effects
Use counterbalancing to distribute order effects evenly:

Half participants: Images first, then Words
Half participants: Words first, then Images

title: Within-Groups Design
text:
Related Concepts

Between-Groups Design
Counterbalancing
Paired t-test (the analysis typically used)

title: Within-Groups Design
text:
DataLab Connection
Several DataLab activities use within-groups designs:

Pre-Post Survey: Each participant rates mood, energy, and stress before AND after the session — classic pre-post repeated measures
Reflex Test: The same participant completes 5 trials, demonstrating practice effects across repeated measures
Time Warp: Each participant completes multiple estimation tasks (time, visual, tactile)

title: Correlational Design
text: A correlational design measures the relationship between two or more variables without manipulating any of them. It examines how variables naturally co-vary.

title: Correlational Design
text: A correlational design measures the relationship between two or more variables without manipulating any of them. It examines how variables naturally co-vary.

title: Correlational Design
text:
Why Use Correlational Designs?
When you cannot manipulate the IV:

Ethical constraints (can’t make people smoke)
Practical constraints (can’t change someone’s age)
Natural phenomena (can’t control earthquakes)

When you want to study real-world relationships:

More ecologically valid
Natural setting
No artificial manipulation

title: Correlational Design
text:
The Causation Problem
Correlation: A and B are related

Possible explanations:
1. A → B         A causes B
2. B → A         B causes A
3. C → A, B      Third variable causes both
4. Coincidence   No real relationship

CANNOT determine which is true!

title: Correlational Design
text:
Third Variable Problem
Example: Ice cream sales correlate with drowning deaths.

Does ice cream cause drowning? No!
Hot weather (third variable) causes both

title: Correlational Design
text:

Avoid

“X causes Y”

“X affects Y”
“X is related to Y”


“X leads to Y”
“X correlates with Y”

title: Correlational Design

DataLab Connection
The Frontal Lob station is a correlational study: participants rate their own throwing ability (1–10), then perform the task. We correlate self-rating with actual performance. This is correlational because we measure both variables but don’t manipulate either — we cannot conclude that self-belief causes performance (or vice versa).

title: Random Assignment
text: Random assignment (randomisation) is the process of allocating participants to experimental conditions using chance, ensuring each participant has an equal probability of being assigned to any condition.

# Assign 60 participants to two groups

# Method 1: Random sample

# Method 2: Random numbers
group <- ifelse(runif(n) < 0.5, "A", "B")

title: Counterbalancing
text: Counterbalancing is a technique used in within-groups designs to distribute order effects evenly across conditions. Different participants experience conditions in different orders.

title: Counterbalancing
text: Counterbalancing is a technique used in within-groups designs to distribute order effects evenly across conditions. Different participants experience conditions in different orders.

title: Counterbalancing
text:
Why Counterbalancing Matters
In within-groups designs, the order in which conditions are presented can affect performance through:

Practice effects: Performance improves with repetition
Fatigue effects: Performance declines over time
Carryover effects: One condition influences the next

Complete Counterbalancing

4th

More efficient than complete counterbalancing for many conditions.


Reverse Counterbalancing (ABBA)
Simple approach for two conditions:
First half:   A → B
Second half:  B → A
This controls for linear trends (e.g., steady fatigue).

title: Counterbalancing
text:
Implementation
Sample: N = 40 participants
Conditions: 2 (Visual, Auditory)

Random assignment to order:
  - 20 participants: Visual first, then Auditory
  - 20 participants: Auditory first, then Visual

Analysis: Include order as a factor to check for effects

title: Counterbalancing
text:
R Code Example
# Create counterbalanced design
set.seed(42)
n <- 40
participants <- 1:n

# Assign to orders
orders <- rep(c("AB", "BA"), each = n/2)
orders <- sample(orders)  # Randomise assignment

design <- tibble(
  participant_id = participants,
  order = orders,
  first_condition = ifelse(order == "AB", "Visual", "Auditory"),
  second_condition = ifelse(order == "AB", "Auditory", "Visual")
)

# Check balance
table(design$order)

# Analyse including order
model <- aov(dv ~ condition * order + Error(participant_id/condition), data = mydata)

title: Counterbalancing
text:
Checking for Order Effects
Always test whether order affected results:

Include order as a between-subjects factor
Test the condition × order interaction
If significant, order effects may be present

title: Between-Groups Design

If probability very low (p < .05), reject null

title: Variance
text: Variance measures the average squared deviation of data points from the mean. It quantifies how spread out the values in a dataset are.

title: Variance
text: Variance measures the average squared deviation of data points from the mean. It quantifies how spread out the values in a dataset are.

title: Variance
text:
Formula
Sample variance:
\[s^2 = \frac{\sum_{i=1}^{n}(X_i - \bar{X})^2}{n-1}\]
Population variance:
\[\sigma^2 = \frac{\sum_{i=1}^{N}(X_i - \mu)^2}{N}\]
Note: Sample formula uses n-1 (Bessel’s correction) for unbiased estimation.

title: Variance
text:
Calculation Steps

Calculate the mean of the data
Subtract the mean from each value (deviations)
Square each deviation
Sum the squared deviations
Divide by n-1 (for sample) or N (for population)

title: Variance
text:
Properties



Property
Description




Always positive
Squared values can’t be negative


Units squared
If data in ms, variance in ms²


Sensitive to outliers
Squaring amplifies extreme values


Foundation for SD
Standard deviation = √variance

title: Variance
text:
Why Square the Deviations?

Raw deviations sum to zero (cancel out)
Squaring makes all values positive
Gives more weight to larger deviations
Has useful mathematical properties

title: Variance
text:
Interpretation



Variance
Interpretation




Small
Values cluster near the mean


Large
Values spread widely from mean


Zero
All values identical

title: Variance
text:
R Code Example
# Sample variance
var(scores)

# With missing values
var(scores, na.rm = TRUE)

# Population variance (divide by n, not n-1)
mean((scores - mean(scores))^2)

# Relationship to SD
var(scores) == sd(scores)^2

title: Variance
text:

Variance
Standard Deviation




Squared units
Original units


Harder to interpret
Easier to interpret


Mathematically convenient

title: Type II Error
text: A Type II error occurs when we fail to reject the null hypothesis when it is actually false. We conclude there is no effect when there really is one. This is also called a “false negative.”

title: Type II Error
text: A Type II error occurs when we fail to reject the null hypothesis when it is actually false. We conclude there is no effect when there really is one. This is also called a “false negative.”

title: Type II Error
text:

Reality

Decision: Don’t Reject H₀

title: Type II Error
text:
Probability of Type II Error

Denoted by β (beta)
Typically ranges from .10 to .20
Related to statistical power: Power = 1 - β

\[P(\text{Type II Error}) = \beta\]

title: Type II Error
text:
Real-World Example
Drug trial:

H₀: Drug has no effect
H₁: Drug has an effect

Type II error: Concluding the drug doesn’t work when it actually does
Consequence: Effective treatment never gets approved

text:

Reducing β increases α

title: Type II Error
text:
DataLab Connection
With small samples at DataLab stations, Type II errors are a real concern. A non-significant result might mean no effect exists, OR that we lacked the power to detect it. Always consider sample size when interpreting null results.

title: Significance Level
text: The significance level (α, alpha) is the threshold probability used to decide whether to reject the null hypothesis. It represents the maximum acceptable risk of making a Type I error.

title: Significance Level
text: The significance level (α, alpha) is the threshold probability used to decide whether to reject the null hypothesis. It represents the maximum acceptable risk of making a Type I error.

title: Significance Level
text:
How It Works
Decision rule:

If p-value < α → Reject H₀ (significant)
If p-value ≥ α → Fail to reject H₀ (not significant)

With α = .05:
  p = .03 → Significant (p < .05) ✓
  p = .07 → Not significant (p > .05) ✗

title: Significance Level
text:
Why .05?
The .05 level was popularised by Ronald Fisher and has become convention:

1 in 20 chance of false positive
Balance between Type I and Type II errors
Not a natural law—just a social convention

Pre-registration helps ensure this

title: Experimental Hypothesis
text:

Feature
Description

title: Experimental Hypothesis
text:

Type
Description

Specifies direction

Predicts difference only

title: Experimental Hypothesis
text:
Writing Hypotheses
A good hypothesis:

States the IV and DV clearly
Predicts the relationship
Is operationalised
Is testable


Example
Abstract: “Caffeine affects memory”
Operationalised: “Participants who consume 200mg caffeine will recall significantly more words from a 30-word list than participants who consume a placebo.”

title: Experimental Hypothesis
text:
Hypothesis Testing Logic
State hypotheses
      │
      ▼
H₀: No effect (µ₁ = µ₂)
H₁: Effect exists (µ₁ ≠ µ₂)
      │
      ▼
Collect data
      │
      ▼
Calculate p-value
      │
      ├── p < .05 → Reject H₀, support H₁
      │
      └── p ≥ .05 → Fail to reject H₀

title: Experimental Hypothesis
text:
Important Notes

We never “prove” H₁
We either reject or fail to reject H₀
Supporting H₁ means the data are unlikely under H₀
Non-significant results don’t prove H₀ is true

title: EDS Assignment
text:
Task Structure
You will receive a research scenario with pre-generated R output. Your task is to interpret the output and demonstrate your understanding of the statistical analysis - no coding or hand calculations required.

Section A: Statistical Mechanics (50 marks)

State the researcher’s hypothesis (5 marks)
Identify design type, IV, DV, data type (16-20 marks)
Interpret R descriptive output and report in APA format (10 marks)
Interpret R t.test() output and justify test choice (15 marks)
Full APA results paragraph from R output (5 marks)
NEW: Error detection - identify what’s wrong with a given analysis (5 marks)



Section B: Methods and Theory (50 marks)

Suggest TWO methodological improvements
Discuss individual differences / extensions
Propose a more ecologically valid alternative (minimum half page)

title: Syllabus
text:
Module Description
This module introduces foundation students to the principles of psychological research. You will learn how to design experiments, collect and analyse data, and report findings in accordance with professional standards.
A distinctive feature of this module is DataLab—in Week 11, you generate the dataset you’ll analyse throughout the term. This means you learn statistics using your own data, not abstract examples.

title: Syllabus
text:
Learning Outcomes
On successful completion of this module, you will be able to:

Conceptual Understanding (C)

Identify experimental designs (between-participants, within-participants, matched pairs, correlational)
Distinguish between IVs and DVs
Formulate appropriate hypotheses (one-tailed, two-tailed)
Understand null hypothesis significance testing
Select appropriate statistical tests
Interpret p-values, confidence intervals, and effect sizes
Recognise the difference between correlation and causation
Critically evaluate research claims



Practical Skills (P)

Calculate descriptive statistics by hand
Run t-tests and correlations in R
Produce appropriate data visualisations
Check statistical assumptions
Report results in APA format



Research Skills (R)

Develop research questions
Operationalise variables
Design appropriate methodologies
Collect data systematically
Write research reports
Critique methodological approaches
Consider ecological validity

Group Project
Working in groups is a core part of this module. Later in the term, your group (comprising 4-5 students) will design and run your own study, collect real data, and write it up as a research report. The group project is a substantial part of your assessment, and the quality of your collaboration directly affects your experience and your grade.

Forming Your Groups
In Week 11, you will work in small groups (2-4 students). This matters, so we are having a nice gentle start!
Pay attention to who communicates clearly, who seems enthusiastic, who you can rely on. Consider working with people you feel comfortable working with outside class hours. Your group will work together on labs from Week 16 onwards and on the research project which makes up a large part of this module. It doesn’t mean that you can’t start planning your group members and group working strategy now though!






ImportantChoose Wisely



Group formation is your first opportunity to see how groups naturally assemble and how different people work together. Group work is a VERY psychological phenomenon and the thing we are asked to talk about most often when writing references for jobs or further study.

title: Median
text: The median is the middle value in an ordered dataset. Half the values fall below the median and half fall above. It represents the 50th percentile.

title: Median
text: The median is the middle value in an ordered dataset. Half the values fall below the median and half fall above. It represents the 50th percentile.

title: Median
text:
Calculation
For odd number of values:

Order values from lowest to highest
Median = the middle value

For even number of values:

Order values from lowest to highest
Median = average of the two middle values

title: Median
text:
Formula
\[Median = X_{\frac{n+1}{2}}\] (for odd n)
\[Median = \frac{X_{\frac{n}{2}} + X_{\frac{n}{2}+1}}{2}\] (for even n)

No assumptions about shape

title: Median

Data are skewed

title: Median
text:
Example
Dataset: 2, 5, 7, 8, 12, 15, 150

Mean = 28.4 (pulled up by outlier 150)
Median = 8 (not affected by outlier)

The median better represents the typical value.

title: Null Hypothesis
text:
Why Test the Null?
We can’t directly prove H₁ is true, but we can show H₀ is unlikely:
Logic of hypothesis testing:

1. Assume H₀ is true (no effect)
2. Calculate probability of our data under H₀
3. If probability very low (p < .05):
   → Data unlikely under H₀
   → Reject H₀ in favour of H₁

title: Null Hypothesis
text:

p-value
Decision
Interpretation




p < .05
Reject H₀
Effect likely exists


p ≥ .05
Fail to reject H₀
Insufficient evidence for effect



Important: “Fail to reject H₀” ≠ “Accept H₀”
We never prove H₀ is true; we just lack evidence against it.

Probability

α (usually .05)

title: Type I Error
text: A Type I error occurs when we reject the null hypothesis when it is actually true. We conclude there is an effect when there really isn’t one. This is also called a “false positive.”

title: Type I Error
text: A Type I error occurs when we reject the null hypothesis when it is actually true. We conclude there is an effect when there really isn’t one. This is also called a “false positive.”

title: Type I Error
text:
Understanding the Error



Reality
Decision: Reject H₀
Decision: Don’t Reject H₀




H₀ True (no effect)
Type I Error ❌
Correct ✓


H₀ False (effect exists)
Correct ✓
Type II Error ❌

title: Type I Error
text:
Probability of Type I Error

Denoted by α (alpha)
Conventionally set at .05 (5%)
This is the significance level

\[P(\text{Type I Error}) = \alpha = .05\]
This means: If we run 100 studies where H₀ is true, we’ll incorrectly reject it about 5 times.

title: Type I Error
text:
Real-World Example
Drug trial:

H₀: Drug has no effect
H₁: Drug has an effect

Type I error: Concluding the drug works when it actually doesn’t
Consequence: Ineffective drug gets approved

title: Type I Error
text:
Why .05?
The .05 threshold is a convention, meaning:

We accept a 5% risk of Type I error
We’re 95% confident when rejecting H₀
It’s a balance between too strict and too lenient

title: Type I Error
text:
Reducing Type I Error



Method
Trade-off




Lower α (e.g., .01)
Increases Type II error risk


Bonferroni correction
For multiple comparisons


Pre-registration
Prevents p-hacking


Replication
Confirms findings

title: Type I Error
section: Type I Error and Multiple Testing
text:
Type I Error and Multiple Testing
With 20 tests at α = .05:
\[P(\text{at least one Type I}) = 1 - (1-.05)^{20} = .64\]
64% chance of at least one false positive!
Solution: Adjust α for multiple comparisons.

title: Type I Error
text:
Related Concepts

Type II Error - false negative
Null Hypothesis - what we’re testing
Significance Level - controls Type I error rate
p-value - probability used in decisions

title: Type I Error
text:
DataLab Connection
When analysing DataLab data, remember that a “significant” result has a 5% chance of being a Type I error. Replication and effect sizes help distinguish true effects from false positives.

title: Directional Hypothesis
text: A directional hypothesis (one-tailed) specifies not only that there will be a difference or relationship, but also the direction of that effect.

Feature
Description

One-tailed test
Critical region in one tail only


More specific
Makes a precise prediction


More power
Easier to detect effect in predicted direction

Non-directional
Directional

When to Use Directional Hypotheses

Only interested in effect in one direction

title: Directional Hypothesis
text:
One-Tailed vs. Two-Tailed Tests
Two-tailed (non-directional):
        ┌──2.5%──┐         ┌──2.5%──┐
        │░░░░░░░░│         │░░░░░░░░│
────────┴────────┴─────────┴────────┴────────
       -1.96     0        +1.96

One-tailed (directional, predicting higher):
                           ┌───5%───┐
                           │░░░░░░░░│
───────────────────────────┴────────┴────────
                  0       +1.65

Critical value lower → easier to reach significance

title: Directional Hypothesis
text:
Advantages and Disadvantages







Advantages
Disadvantages




More statistical power
Cannot detect opposite effects


Lower critical value
Must justify direction a priori


Matches specific predictions
Can seem like p-hacking if chosen after data

title: Directional Hypothesis

Important Rule
You must choose directional or non-directional before collecting data. Choosing after seeing the data is inappropriate and inflates Type I error.

Null Hypothesis - what we test against

DataLab Connection
For Reflex Test, a directional hypothesis is appropriate: “Reaction times will be significantly slower in the choice condition than in the simple condition” (based on well-established Hick’s Law).

title: Standard Deviation
text: The standard deviation measures the average distance of data points from the mean. It quantifies the spread or dispersion of values in a dataset.

title: Standard Deviation
text: The standard deviation measures the average distance of data points from the mean. It quantifies the spread or dispersion of values in a dataset.

title: Standard Deviation
text:
Formula
Sample standard deviation:
\[s = \sqrt{\frac{\sum_{i=1}^{n}(X_i - \bar{X})^2}{n-1}}\]
Population standard deviation:
\[\sigma = \sqrt{\frac{\sum_{i=1}^{N}(X_i - \mu)^2}{N}}\]
Note: Sample formula uses n-1 (Bessel’s correction) for unbiased estimation.

title: Standard Deviation
text:
Interpretation



SD value
Interpretation




Small SD
Values clustered near the mean


Large SD
Values spread widely from mean


SD = 0
All values identical

title: Standard Deviation
text:
The 68-95-99.7 Rule
For normally distributed data:
                     ▲
                    ╱│╲
                   ╱ │ ╲
            68%   ╱  │  ╲   
                 ╱   │   ╲
           95%  ╱    │    ╲  
               ╱     │     ╲
          99.7%      │      
──────────┼────┼─────┼─────┼────┼──────►
        -3SD -2SD  -1SD   Mean  +1SD +2SD +3SD

• 68% of values within ±1 SD
• 95% of values within ±2 SD  
• 99.7% of values within ±3 SD

title: Standard Deviation
text:
Calculation Steps

Calculate the mean
Subtract mean from each value (deviations)
Square each deviation
Sum the squared deviations
Divide by n-1 (variance)
Take the square root

title: Standard Deviation
text:
R Code Example
# Standard deviation
sd(scores)

# With missing values
sd(scores, na.rm = TRUE)

# Population SD (divide by n, not n-1)
sqrt(mean((scores - mean(scores))^2))

# Variance (SD squared)
var(scores)

title: Standard Deviation
text:
Reporting (APA Style)

Participants had a mean reaction time of 450 ms (SD = 52).

Always report SD alongside the mean to convey both central tendency and spread.

title: Standard Deviation
text:
Comparing Variability
Coefficient of Variation (for comparing SDs across different scales):
\[CV = \frac{SD}{Mean} \times 100\]

title: Standard Deviation
text:
Related Concepts

Variance - SD squared
Mean - centre of the distribution

title: Standard Deviation
text:
DataLab Connection
Calculate SD for reaction times at the Reflex Test to understand individual consistency. High SD suggests variable performance; low SD suggests consistent responding.

title: Matched Participants Design
text: A matched participants design is a type of between-groups design where participants are paired based on key variables, and then each pair member is randomly assigned to different conditions.

title: Matched Participants Design
text: A matched participants design is a type of between-groups design where participants are paired based on key variables, and then each pair member is randomly assigned to different conditions.

title: Matched Participants Design
text:
How It Works
1. Identify key variable(s) to match on
2. Pair participants with similar scores
3. Randomly assign one from each pair to each condition

Example matching on IQ:
Pair 1: Person A (IQ=105) → Condition 1
        Person B (IQ=103) → Condition 2
Pair 2: Person C (IQ=118) → Condition 1
        Person D (IQ=120) → Condition 2

title: Matched Participants Design
text:
Key Characteristics



Feature
Description




Matched pairs

Random assignment
Within each pair


Between-groups
Different people in each condition


Reduced variance
Controls for matched variable

title: Matched Participants Design
text:
Matching Variables
Choose variables likely to affect the DV:



Study Type
Match On

Reaction time

Academic intervention
Prior achievement


Drug trial

title: Matched Participants Design
text:
Advantages

Reduces individual differences for matched variables
More powerful than simple between-groups
No order effects (unlike within-groups)
Can use independent t-test analysis

title: Matched Participants Design
text:
Disadvantages

Time-consuming to match
May lose participants who can’t be matched
Only controls for variables you match on
Requires large pool to find good matches

title: Matched Participants Design
text:
Analysis
Use a paired t-test (treating matched pairs as related samples) or independent t-test (treating as independent groups):
# As matched pairs (more powerful)
t.test(condition1, condition2, paired = TRUE)

# As independent groups
t.test(score ~ condition, data = mydata)

DataLab doesn’t use pre-matching, but you could create matched pairs post-hoc for analysis—for example, matching participants by age before comparing reaction times across conditions.

title: Confounding Variable
text:
A confounding variable (or confound) is a variable that:

Varies systematically with the independent variable
Also affects the dependent variable

This makes it impossible to determine whether changes in the DV are due to the IV or the confound.

title: Confounding Variable
text:
A confounding variable (or confound) is a variable that:

Also affects the dependent variable

text:

                    Confound
                   ╱        ╲
                  ↓          ↓

Strategy
