At Lady Luck, risk-taking behaviour and gender may be confounded—if more males choose risky options, we can’t tell if it’s gender or some other variable associated with gender that drives the effect.

title: Practice Effect
text: A practice effect is the improvement in performance that occurs when participants become more familiar with a task through repetition, independent of the experimental manipulation.

title: Practice Effect
text: A practice effect is the improvement in performance that occurs when participants become more familiar with a task through repetition, independent of the experimental manipulation.

title: Practice Effect
text:
Why Practice Effects Occur

Learning the task requirements
Developing efficient strategies
Reduced anxiety/unfamiliarity
Motor skill improvement
Understanding response options

title: Practice Effect
text:
Example
Testing memory with two techniques:



Order
Technique
Score
Interpretation




1st
Method A
12/20
Baseline


2nd
Method B
16/20
Better method or practice?



The 4-point improvement could be:

Participant learned the task

title: Practice Effect
text:
Controlling Practice Effects

1. Counterbalancing
Group 1: Method A → Method B
Group 2: Method B → Method A

If Method B still better in both orders → genuine effect


2. Practice Trials
Give participants practice before the real task:
Practice trials (not scored)
    ↓
Condition A (scored)
    ↓
Condition B (scored)


3. Long Delays Between Conditions
Allows any practice benefit to dissipate.


4. Different Stimuli
Use different (but equivalent) materials in each condition.

title: Practice Effect
text:
Distinguishing Practice from True Effects
Check the condition × order interaction:
# If this interaction is significant, order matters
summary(aov(score ~ condition * order + Error(id/condition)))
                    Order
                 A-first    B-first
Condition A        12         14      ← Both improve
Condition B        18         16      ← with practice

If B > A in both orders → genuine condition effect

title: Practice Effect
text:

title: Practice Effect
text:
DataLab Connection
The Reflex Test station directly demonstrates practice effects: participants catch a dropped ruler across 5 trials. Reaction times typically improve from Trial 1 to Trial 5 as participants learn the timing and develop better strategies. A paired t-test comparing Trial 1 vs Trial 5 can quantify the practice effect.

title: Order Effects
text: Order effects occur in within-groups designs when performance changes simply because of the sequence in which conditions are experienced, rather than the conditions themselves.

title: Order Effects
text: Order effects occur in within-groups designs when performance changes simply because of the sequence in which conditions are experienced, rather than the conditions themselves.

text:
Types of Order Effects








Effect
Description
Example

Faster responses in later trials

More errors when tired

Mood from task 1 influences task 2

Noticing differences after practice

text:
Visual Representation

Performance ▲
            │        ●
            │     ●
            │  ●
            │●
            └──────────────► Time/Trials
            Condition A → Condition B

            │●
            │  ●
            │     ●
            │        ●

title: Order Effects
text:
The Problem
In a within-groups design:

If everyone does A then B
And B scores higher than A
Is it because B is genuinely better?
Or because participants improved with practice?

We can’t tell! The effect is confounded with order.

title: Order Effects
text:
Solutions

1. Counterbalancing
Half do A→B, half do B→A
Group 1: A → B
Group 2: B → A

Order effects balance out across groups


2. Randomisation
Randomise condition order for each participant


3. Include Order as a Factor
Analyse whether order interacted with condition:
# Check for order effects
model <- aov(dv ~ condition * order + Error(participant_id/condition))
summary(model)

title: Order Effects
text:
Detecting Order Effects
Signs that order effects may be present:

Significant condition × order interaction
Performance systematically changes across trials
Large difference between first and last conditions

title: Order Effects

title: Order Effects

DataLab Connection
At the Reflex Test station, reaction times typically improve across trials due to practice. Counterbalancing the order of simple vs. choice conditions helps separate true condition differences from practice effects.

title: Mann-Whitney U Test
text: The Mann-Whitney U test (also called Wilcoxon rank-sum test) is a non-parametric test that compares the distributions of two independent groups. It tests whether one group tends to have larger values than the other.

title: Mann-Whitney U Test
text: The Mann-Whitney U test (also called Wilcoxon rank-sum test) is a non-parametric test that compares the distributions of two independent groups. It tests whether one group tends to have larger values than the other.

title: Mann-Whitney U Test
text:
When to Use
Use a Mann-Whitney U test when:

Comparing two independent groups
Data are ordinal, or continuous but non-normal
Sample sizes are small
Outliers are present
Assumptions of the independent t-test are violated

title: Mann-Whitney U Test
text:
How It Works

Combine all observations from both groups
Rank all values from lowest to highest
Sum the ranks for each group
Compare rank sums to expected values

title: Mann-Whitney U Test
text:
The Test Statistic
\[U = n_1 n_2 + \frac{n_1(n_1 + 1)}{2} - R_1\]
Where:

\(n_1, n_2\) = sample sizes of groups
\(R_1\) = sum of ranks in group 1

title: Mann-Whitney U Test
text:
Assumptions



Assumption
Notes




Independence
Observations between groups independent


Ordinal data
At minimum, can rank the values


Similar shape
Distributions have similar shape

title: Mann-Whitney U Test
text:
Effect Size
Calculate rank-biserial correlation (\(r\)):
\[r = \frac{2U}{n_1 n_2} - 1\]



r value
Interpretation




0.1
Small effect


0.3
Medium effect


0.5
Large effect

title: Mann-Whitney U Test
text:
R Code Example
# Mann-Whitney U test (Wilcoxon rank-sum)

# With exact p-value for small samples

title: Pearson’s r
text: Pearson’s r (also called Pearson’s product-moment correlation coefficient) measures the strength and direction of the linear relationship between two continuous variables. It is the parametric correlation test.

title: Pearson’s r

When to Use

title: Pearson’s r
text:
The Formula
\[r = \frac{\sum(X_i - \bar{X})(Y_i - \bar{Y})}{\sqrt{\sum(X_i - \bar{X})^2 \sum(Y_i - \bar{Y})^2}}\]
Or using z-scores:
\[r = \frac{\sum z_X z_Y}{n-1}\]

title: Pearson’s r

r² tells us the proportion of variance explained:

title: Wilcoxon Signed-Rank Test
text: The Wilcoxon signed-rank test is a non-parametric test that compares two related samples, matched samples, or repeated measurements on a single sample. It tests whether the distribution of differences is symmetric about zero.

title: Wilcoxon Signed-Rank Test
text: The Wilcoxon signed-rank test is a non-parametric test that compares two related samples, matched samples, or repeated measurements on a single sample. It tests whether the distribution of differences is symmetric about zero.

text:

title: Wilcoxon Signed-Rank Test
text:
How It Works

Calculate the difference for each pair
Rank the absolute values of differences
Assign signs (+ or -) based on difference direction
Sum positive and negative ranks separately
Compare to expected distribution

title: Wilcoxon Signed-Rank Test

\[W = \min(W^+, W^-)\]
Where:

\(W^-\) = sum of negative ranks

title: Station 3: Time Warp
text:
Station Overview
The Time Warp station investigates how accurately we perceive time and physical dimensions. Participants estimate a 60-second interval, visually estimate line lengths, tactilely estimate string lengths (with eyes closed), and guess the room temperature. This station generates error scores that reveal systematic biases in human perception.

title: Station 3: Time Warp
text:
What Participants Do

Part A: 60-Second Estimation

Close your eyes
When your partner says “Start”, sense time passing
Say “Stop” when you think 60 seconds have passed
Partner records the actual time elapsed



Part B: Visual Estimation (Lines)

Look at Line Card A — estimate its length in cm
Repeat with Line Card B



Part C: Tactile Estimation (Strings)

Feel String 1 with eyes closed — estimate its length in cm
Repeat with String 2



Part D: Temperature Estimation

Guess the current room temperature in °C

title: Station 3: Time Warp
text:
Research Questions

Do people systematically over- or under-estimate 60 seconds?


Is visual estimation more accurate than tactile estimation?


Does counting during time estimation improve accuracy?

title: Station 3: Time Warp
text:
Experimental Design



Element
Description




Design
Within-groups (multiple estimation tasks)


IV
Estimation modality (time, visual, tactile, temperature)


DV
Estimation error (estimate − actual)


Controls
Consistent environment, no visible clocks

TipWhy Do We Underestimate Time?



When waiting without distraction, people often feel time passing more slowly than it actually is, leading them to say “stop” before 60 seconds have elapsed. This is called temporal underestimation.

text:

Paired comparison: Visual vs tactile estimation accuracy

Mean and SD of each error score
Proportion of over- vs under-estimators

Exploratory analyses:

Does counting improve time estimation accuracy?
Compare music vs silence conditions on time perception

title: Station 3: Time Warp
text:
R Code Starter
# Load data
datalab <- read_csv("datalab_data.csv")

# Calculate time error
datalab <- datalab |>
  mutate(time_error = time_estimate_sec - 60)

# One-sample t-test: Is mean error different from 0?
t.test(datalab$time_error, mu = 0)

# Descriptive statistics
datalab |>
  summarise(
    mean_error = mean(time_error, na.rm = TRUE),
    sd_error = sd(time_error, na.rm = TRUE),
    prop_under = mean(time_error < 0, na.rm = TRUE)
  )

# Compare counters vs non-counters
datalab |>
  group_by(time_counting) |>
  summarise(
    mean_error = mean(time_error, na.rm = TRUE),
    sd_error = sd(time_error, na.rm = TRUE)
  )

# Visualise time estimation
library(ggplot2)
ggplot(datalab, aes(x = time_estimate_sec)) +
  geom_histogram(binwidth = 5, fill = "#275882", colour = "white") +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 60, colour = "#EA8439", linewidth = 1.5, linetype = "dashed") +
  labs(
    x = "Time Estimate (seconds)",
    y = "Count",
    title = "60-Second Estimation Distribution",
    subtitle = "Dashed line = actual 60 seconds"
  )

This station demonstrates:

Within-Groups Design — same participant across multiple tasks

title: Station 3: Time Warp
text:
Tips for Facilitators

Ensure participants cannot see clocks or phones during time estimation
For tactile estimation, participants should keep eyes fully closed
Note if participants use counting strategies — this is valuable data
Actual measurements (line lengths, string lengths, room temp) should be recorded beforehand

title: Pre-Post Survey
text: The Pre-Post Survey measures participants’ mood, energy, and stress levels before and after completing the DataLab stations. This creates a classic within-subjects pre-post design, allowing us to test whether the DataLab experience affected how participants feel.

title: Pre-Post Survey
text: The Pre-Post Survey measures participants’ mood, energy, and stress levels before and after completing the DataLab stations. This creates a classic within-subjects pre-post design, allowing us to test whether the DataLab experience affected how participants feel.

title: Pre-Post Survey
text:
R Code Starter
# Load data
datalab <- read_csv("datalab_data.csv")

# Calculate change scores
datalab <- datalab |>
  mutate(
    mood_change = mood_post - mood_pre,
    energy_change = energy_post - energy_pre,
    stress_change = stress_post - stress_pre
  )

# Descriptive statistics
datalab |>
  summarise(
    mood_pre_mean = mean(mood_pre, na.rm = TRUE),
    mood_post_mean = mean(mood_post, na.rm = TRUE),
    mood_change_mean = mean(mood_change, na.rm = TRUE)
  )

# Paired t-test for mood
t.test(datalab$mood_post, datalab$mood_pre, paired = TRUE)

# Visualise change
library(ggplot2)

title: Station 5: Lady Luck
text:
Station Overview
The Lady Luck station investigates how well humans can generate and perceive randomness. Participants generate “random” numbers, roll dice, and flip coins. The key finding: humans are bad at being random — we systematically avoid repetitions and produce sequences that are “too varied” to be truly random.

title: Station 5: Lady Luck
text:
What Participants Do

Part A: Random Number Generation

Say 20 “random” numbers between 1 and 10 aloud
Partner records each number
Try to be as random as possible!



Part B: Dice Rolling

Predict: Will you roll more 6s than expected by chance?
Roll the die 10 times
Record each outcome (1–6)



Part C: Coin Flipping

Flip a coin 10 times
Record each outcome (Heads or Tails)
Note the longest run of the same outcome

title: Station 5: Lady Luck
text:

Do human-generated “random” numbers differ from true random?


Do people roll more or fewer 6s than expected (1.67 out of 10)?


Do people expect fewer runs in random sequences than actually occur?

NoteThe Psychology of Randomness

title: Station 5: Lady Luck
text:
R Code Starter
# Load data
datalab <- read_csv("datalab_data.csv")

# Calculate mean of random numbers (wide to long)
library(tidyr)
datalab_rand <- datalab |>
  select(participant_id, rand_num1:rand_num20) |>
  pivot_longer(
    cols = starts_with("rand_num"),
    names_to = "position",
    values_to = "number"
  )

# Mean per participant
rand_means <- datalab_rand |>
  group_by(participant_id) |>
  summarise(rand_mean = mean(number, na.rm = TRUE))

# One-sample t-test: Is mean different from 5.5?
t.test(rand_means$rand_mean, mu = 5.5)

# Count repetitions (adjacent same numbers)
count_reps <- function(nums) {
  sum(nums[-1] == nums[-length(nums)], na.rm = TRUE)
}

datalab <- datalab |>
  rowwise() |>
  mutate(rand_repeats = count_reps(c_across(rand_num1:rand_num20)))

# Compare repetitions to expected (~2)
t.test(datalab$rand_repeats, mu = 2)

# Visualise digit frequencies
ggplot(datalab_rand, aes(x = factor(number))) +
  geom_bar(fill = "#275882") +
  geom_hline(yintercept = nrow(datalab_rand) / 10,
             colour = "#EA8439", linewidth = 1, linetype = "dashed") +
  labs(
    x = "Number Generated",
    y = "Frequency",
    title = "Human 'Random' Number Distribution",
    subtitle = "Dashed line = expected if truly random"
  )

title: Station 1: Reflex Test
text:
Station Overview
The Reflex Test measures how quickly your nervous system can respond to a visual stimulus. Using a simple ruler-drop task, participants catch a falling ruler and convert the distance caught to reaction time in milliseconds. This station demonstrates the practice effect — reaction times typically improve across repeated trials.

title: Station 1: Reflex Test
text:
What Participants Do

Partner A holds the ruler at the 30cm mark, letting it hang vertically
Partner B positions thumb and finger at the 0cm mark — without touching!
Partner A drops the ruler without warning (within 5 seconds)
Partner B catches it as fast as possible
Read the distance in cm at the top of your thumb
Complete 5 trials, then swap roles

title: Station 1: Reflex Test
text:

Do reaction times improve with practice across 5 trials?


Is there a difference between dominant and non-dominant hand reaction times?


Do individual differences (sleep, caffeine) predict reaction time?

title: Station 1: Reflex Test
text:
R Code Starter
# Load data
datalab <- read_csv("datalab_data.csv")

# Convert cm to ms using physics formula
cm_to_ms <- function(cm) {
  sqrt(2 * (cm / 100) / 9.81) * 1000
}

# Calculate RT in milliseconds
datalab <- datalab |>
  mutate(
    rt_trial1_ms = cm_to_ms(rt_trial1_cm),
    rt_trial2_ms = cm_to_ms(rt_trial2_cm),
    rt_trial3_ms = cm_to_ms(rt_trial3_cm),
    rt_trial4_ms = cm_to_ms(rt_trial4_cm),
    rt_trial5_ms = cm_to_ms(rt_trial5_cm)
  )

# Mean RT across trials
datalab <- datalab |>
  rowwise() |>
  mutate(rt_mean_ms = mean(c(rt_trial1_ms, rt_trial2_ms, rt_trial3_ms,
                             rt_trial4_ms, rt_trial5_ms), na.rm = TRUE))

# Paired t-test: Trial 1 vs Trial 5
t.test(datalab$rt_trial1_ms, datalab$rt_trial5_ms, paired = TRUE)

# Visualise practice effect
library(tidyr)
library(ggplot2)

datalab |>
  select(participant_id, rt_trial1_ms:rt_trial5_ms) |>
  pivot_longer(cols = -participant_id,
               names_to = "trial",
               values_to = "rt_ms") |>
  mutate(trial = parse_number(trial)) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = trial, y = rt_ms, group = participant_id)) +
  geom_line(alpha = 0.3) +
  geom_smooth(aes(group = 1), method = "lm", se = TRUE, colour = "#275882") +
  labs(x = "Trial", y = "Reaction Time (ms)",
       title = "Practice Effect in Reflex Test")

The Problem with Common Sense

“Opposites attract”

Common sense often gives contradictory answers. Science provides a systematic way to find out what’s actually true.

title: Introduction to Research Methods & Experimental Design

Step 2: The Hypothesis

A hypothesis is a specific, testable prediction about what you expect to find.

Good hypothesis:

“Participants will tell more lies per conversation when communicating via text message compared to face-to-face.”

Not a hypothesis:

“I wonder if texting affects lying.”

Who will you study? (participants)
What will you measure? (variables)
How will you measure it? (methods)
What comparisons will you make? (design)


We’ll spend most of this module on this step.

Follow your plan precisely

Minimise errors and bias

Step 5: Analyse Data

Statistics are tools for finding patterns in data and determining whether those patterns are meaningful.

This is where R comes in — and what you’ll learn in the labs.

What do the findings mean?
Do they support the hypothesis?
What are the limitations?

title: Chapter 2: DataLab Foundations
text:
Reflecting on Data Collection
DataLab was probably your first experience collecting psychological data. You may have noticed things didn’t always go smoothly:

Instructions weren’t always clear
Timing was tricky
Partners did things differently
The environment was distracting
Recording data while running a task was harder than expected

This is normal. In fact, these challenges are exactly why research methods matter. Understanding what can go wrong helps you:

Appreciate why standardised procedures exist
Interpret your own data more thoughtfully
Design better studies in the future

As you read about each task below, think about what happened during your data collection. What might have affected your measurements?

title: Chapter 2: DataLab Foundations
text:
What You Measured
DataLab included a group memory test plus five tasks measuring different aspects of human cognition and behaviour. For each task, we’ll cover the psychological background and then consider methodological issues.

Task 1: Reaction Time (Reflex Test)

Reaction time is the interval between a stimulus and your response to it. In the ruler-drop task, we measured simple reaction time — how quickly you could respond to a single, expected stimulus.
The physics is elegant: when you catch a falling ruler, the distance it fell before you caught it tells us how long your reaction took. Using the equation for free-falling objects (d = ½gt²), we can convert centimetres into milliseconds.






NoteWhy It Matters



Reaction time is one of the most reliable measures in psychology. Your data will show how consistent (or variable) human performance is, even on simple tasks. We can also look for practice effects — did you get faster across trials?








WarningMethodological Considerations



Measurement error:

Was the ruler held at exactly the same height each time?
Did the participant’s fingers start in exactly the same position?
Was it always clear where to read the catch point?

Potential biases:

Anticipation: Did you start to predict when the drop would happen?
Practice effects: Did you genuinely get faster, or just better at anticipating?
Hand dominance: We only tested one hand — would results differ for the other?

Procedural issues:

How consistent was your partner’s dropping technique?
Were there distractions (noise, movement) that affected some trials?
Did everyone follow the same instructions?





Memory Test: Mind Palace

The memory task measured working memory — how many items you can hold in mind while performing another task.
Miller (1956) famously proposed that we can hold about 7 ± 2 items in short-term memory — the “magical number seven.” But the distraction task (maths problems) interferes with rehearsal, so performance typically drops.
We’ll also examine the serial position effect: people tend to remember words from the beginning of a list (primacy) and end of a list (recency) better than the middle. Your position-by-position recall data will let us test this pattern.






WarningMethodological Considerations



Measurement error:

Were the words presented at the same speed for everyone?
Could everyone hear clearly from where they were sitting?
Was the recall period the same length for all participants?

Potential biases:

Prior exposure: Had you seen any of the words recently?
Language background: Were the words equally familiar to everyone?
Strategy use: Some people use chunking or visualisation — should we control for this?

Procedural issues:

Was the distraction task equally difficult for everyone?
Did the timing between presentation and recall vary?
How was recall scored? (exact spelling? close enough?)





Task 2: Time and Magnitude Perception (Time Warp)

How accurately do we perceive time? Research shows that our internal clocks are surprisingly inaccurate and can be influenced by many factors.
This station measured three types of estimation:

Time estimation — How accurately could you judge 60 seconds?
Visual magnitude estimation — How accurately could you judge line lengths by looking?
Tactile magnitude estimation — How accurately could you judge lengths by touch alone?







TipCross-Modal Comparison



By comparing visual and tactile estimation, we can explore whether some senses are more accurate than others for judging physical properties.








WarningMethodological Considerations



Measurement error:

When exactly did the stopwatch start? When you said “start” or when your partner pressed it?
How precisely were line lengths measured?
Was string tension consistent across tactile trials?

Potential biases:

Counting: Did you count seconds in your head? (This is a strategy, not pure time perception)
Anchoring: Did early estimates influence later ones?
Expectation: Did you adjust estimates based on feedback?

Procedural issues:

Could you see any clocks or time displays?
Were there environmental cues (regular sounds, movements)?
Was it quiet enough to concentrate?





Task 3: Psychic Staring (Sixth Sense)

Can humans detect when they’re being watched? This is a testable empirical question!
The staring detection task uses signal detection theory:

Hits: Correctly detecting when someone IS staring
False alarms: Saying “staring” when they’re NOT
Misses: Saying “not staring” when they ARE
Correct rejections: Correctly detecting when they’re NOT staring

If people cannot actually detect staring, we’d expect performance to be at chance level (about 50% correct, or 3 out of 6 trials).






WarningMethodological Considerations



Measurement error:

Could you detect your partner through peripheral vision?
Were there sounds or movements that gave it away?
Was “staring” defined consistently? (How long? How intense?)

Potential biases:

Response bias: Did you tend to say “yes” or “no” more often?
Pattern-seeking: Did you assume alternating patterns?
Confirmation bias: Did you interpret ambiguous feelings as evidence for your guess?

Procedural issues:

How reliably did your partner randomise staring/not-staring?
Was the duration of each trial consistent?
Could other people in the room affect the “being watched” feeling?





Task 4: Randomness (Lady Luck)

Humans are notoriously bad at generating random sequences. When asked to produce “random” numbers, people:

Avoid repeating the same number twice in a row (even though true randomness includes repetitions)
Avoid patterns (even though random sequences often contain streaks)
Favour certain numbers (often 7!)

This station also included dice rolling and coin flipping, which let us compare true random outcomes (from dice/coins) with human-generated random sequences.






NoteThe Gambler’s Fallacy



Many people believe that after a streak of heads, tails is “due.” This is false — each flip is independent. Your data will likely show longer runs than most people expect!








WarningMethodological Considerations



Measurement error:

Were all 20 numbers recorded correctly?
Were dice rolls and coin flips recorded accurately?
How were “runs” counted? Was this consistent?

Potential biases:

Number preferences: Did cultural factors affect which numbers felt “random”?
Avoidance of repetition: This is a known bias — but did you try to overcome it?
Anchoring: Did your previous number influence your next choice?

Procedural issues:

Was there time pressure that affected your choices?
Did you understand what “random” meant in this context?
Were the dice fair? Were coins flipped properly?





Task 5: Metacognition (Frontal Lob)

Metacognition is thinking about your own thinking — including how well you know your own abilities.
The throwing task measured calibration: the match between your self-assessed ability and your actual performance.

Overconfidence: Rating yourself higher than your performance
Underconfidence: Rating yourself lower than your performance
Well-calibrated: Your rating matches your performance

Research consistently shows that people are poorly calibrated — often overconfident about easy tasks and underconfident about hard ones.






WarningMethodological Considerations



Measurement error:

How were successful throws defined? What about balls that bounced in?
Who counted the successes — participant or tester?
Was counting accurate across 10 throws?

Potential biases:

Self-serving bias: Did you rate yourself higher because you wanted to be good?
Social desirability: Did having a partner watching affect your self-rating?
Anchoring: Did the 1-10 scale influence what felt like a “reasonable” rating?

Procedural issues:

Was the throwing distance the same for everyone?
Was the target positioned consistently?
Did throwing technique vary (overarm, underarm)?

title: Chapter 2: DataLab Foundations
text:
The Pre-Post Design
DataLab used a within-subjects design to measure mood change. You rated your mood, energy, and stress both before and after the stations.
This design is powerful because each person serves as their own control. By comparing your “before” to your “after,” we eliminate individual differences — we’re measuring change within you, not differences between people.






ImportantTeaching Application



When we learn about paired t-tests, we’ll analyse whether DataLab systematically affected mood, energy, or stress. Did participation make people feel better? Worse? More or less stressed?

title: Chapter 2: DataLab Foundations
text:
Why This Matters
You’ve just experienced something important: collecting data is hard.
The methodological issues above aren’t criticisms — they’re reality. Even professional researchers face these challenges. The difference is that professionals:

Use standardised procedures — detailed protocols that specify exactly how to do each step
Define variables operationally — clear definitions of what counts as a “catch” or a “success”
Train testers — so everyone administers tasks the same way
Control the environment — quiet rooms, consistent setups, minimal distractions
Check inter-rater reliability — do two testers recording the same event get the same result?

When we analyse your DataLab data, we’ll need to keep these limitations in mind. Some variability in the data reflects genuine individual differences. Some reflects measurement error and procedural inconsistencies.
Learning to tell the difference is what research methods is all about.

title: Chapter 2: DataLab Foundations
section: Why We Generated Our Own Data
text:
Why We Generated Our Own Data

Learning with Real Data
When we analyse data you’ve generated:

You understand what the numbers represent
You can connect statistics to real experiences
The results are genuinely unknown (not textbook examples)



Experiencing Both Roles
Acting as both participant and tester taught you:

The importance of standardised procedures
How instructions affect behaviour
Why research protocols exist



Understanding Limitations
Having collected data yourself, you now understand:

Why researchers obsess over procedures
How small variations can affect results
That “messy data” is normal — interpretation requires care

title: Chapter 2: DataLab Foundations
text:
How You Worked in Pairs
At each task, you worked with a partner:

One person was the participant (completed the task)
One person was the tester (administered the task, recorded data)
Then you swapped roles

This meant everyone experienced both perspectives.
You received a sequence card telling you which tasks to complete in which order.

title: Chapter 2: DataLab Foundations
text:
Key Terms



Term
Related Concepts




Reaction time
simple RT, catch distance, milliseconds

title: Chapter 3: Research Design Framework
text:
Part 1: The Building Blocks — Variables

What Is a Variable?
A variable is anything that can vary — any characteristic, number, or quantity that can take different values.
In the DataLab:

Memory scores varied (some people remembered 4 words, others 8)
Mood ratings varied (some felt 3/10, others 8/10)
Reaction times varied (some caught the ruler quickly, others slowly)



Independent and Dependent Variables
In experimental research, we distinguish between two types of variables:

Independent Variable (IV): What the researcher manipulates or controls — the presumed cause.
Dependent Variable (DV): What the researcher measures — the outcome that may be affected.

The DV depends on the IV. We’re asking: Does the outcome depend on the condition?


DataLab Example: Memory Task
In the memory experiment:

IV: Word type (abstract vs concrete)
DV: Number of words recalled (0-10)

Lab A saw abstract words (justice, freedom, wisdom). Lab B saw concrete words (chair, river, mountain). The researcher manipulated which words you saw — that’s the IV.
What we measured — how many words you recalled — is the DV. We wanted to know if recall depended on the word type.


When There Is No IV
Not all research involves manipulation. Sometimes we simply measure two things and look at their relationship.
In the Frontal Lob task, you rated how good you thought you’d be at throwing (1-10), and then we measured your actual accuracy. Neither was manipulated — we just measured both.






ImportantKey Insight



When there’s no manipulation, there’s no IV. This is called a correlational design, and we’ll cover it shortly.




Data Types
The DV can be measured in different ways:








Data Type
Description
Example




Continuous
Can take any value (including decimals)
Reaction time (245.3ms)


Discrete
Whole numbers only (counts)
Words recalled (7)


Categorical
Categories with no numerical order
Lab group (A or B)


Ordinal
Categories with an order
Rating (1-10 scale)



In the DataLab:

Memory score is discrete (you can’t recall 6.5 words)
Reaction time is continuous (could be 245.3ms or 245.4ms)
Mood rating is ordinal (1-10 scale with order, but intervals may not be equal)

title: Chapter 3: Research Design Framework
text:
Part 2: Design Types
The design refers to how participants are assigned to conditions.

Between-Subjects Design

Between-subjects design: Different participants in each condition.

In the memory experiment, you were in either Lab A (abstract words) or Lab B (concrete words) — never both. Different people were in each condition.
Why “between”? We’re comparing between groups — Lab A people versus Lab B people.
Advantage: No order effects (practice, fatigue, boredom)
Disadvantage: Individual differences may affect results (maybe Lab B just happened to have better memorisers)


Within-Subjects Design

Within-subjects design: The same participants measured in all conditions.

In the pre-post mood survey, you rated your mood before and after the session. The same person provided both data points.
Why “within”? We’re comparing within the same person — your pre-mood versus your post-mood.
Advantage: Each person is their own control! Individual differences are controlled because we’re comparing you to yourself.
Disadvantage: Order effects possible (practice, fatigue)


Within-Subjects Examples from DataLab



Task
Same Person Compared




Pre/Post mood
Before vs after session


Pre/Post energy
Before vs after session


Pre/Post stress
Before vs after session


Frontal Lob
Dominant vs non-dominant hand





Matched Pairs Design

Matched pairs design: Participants are paired on a key characteristic, then one from each pair goes to each condition.

This is a hybrid — different people in each condition (like between-subjects), but they’re matched to be similar (reducing individual difference problems).
Example: Match students by the amount of sleep they reported the night before. Let’s say two participants reported five hours and two participants reported 10 hours. One from each pair gets abstract words, the other gets concrete words. This would allow me to control for sleep quantity (five or ten hours), as I would have each level represented in each group. It means I would have to ask about sleep before allocating to condition, and so is a little bit more complicated in everyday life.


Correlational Design

Correlational design: Measuring the relationship between two variables — no manipulation.

When we measured self-rating and actual throwing performance, we didn’t manipulate either. We simply measured both and asked: Are they related? This could be the same for hours of sleep and memory performance, or any of the personality traits we measured and any other outcome variable.






WarningCritical Point



In correlational designs, there is NO IV. Neither variable is the “cause” — we’re just measuring a relationship.




Summary: Design Types








Design
Key Feature
Example




Between-subjects
Different people in each condition
Lab A vs Lab B


Within-subjects
Same people in all conditions
Pre vs Post mood


Matched pairs
Participants paired, one per condition
Matched by ability


Correlational

Self-rating vs performance

title: Chapter 3: Research Design Framework
text:
Part 3: Writing Hypotheses
A hypothesis is a prediction about what you expect to find.

Experimental vs Null Hypothesis

Experimental hypothesis (H₁ or Ha): Predicts an effect or difference will exist.
Null hypothesis (H₀): Predicts no effect or no difference.

For the memory experiment:

H₁: Concrete words will be easier to remember than abstract words.
H₀: There will be no difference in recall between word types.

Statistical testing works by assuming H₀ is true, then checking if the data is surprising enough to reject that assumption.


One-Tailed vs Two-Tailed

One-tailed hypothesis: Predicts the direction of the effect.
Two-tailed hypothesis: Predicts a difference but not which direction.

One-tailed examples:

“Concrete words will be easier to remember than abstract words” (predicts concrete > abstract)
“Mood will improve after the session” (predicts post > pre)
“Dominant hand will be more accurate than non-dominant hand” (predicts dominant > non-dominant)

Two-tailed examples:

“Word type will affect memory” (could be better or worse)
“Mood will change after the session” (could go up or down)
“There will be a difference in accuracy between hands” (no direction predicted)



When to Use Which?
Use one-tailed when:

Previous research strongly suggests a direction
Your theory predicts a specific direction
You only care about effects in one direction

Use two-tailed when:

You’re uncertain about the direction
Effects in either direction would be interesting
You’re being conservative (harder to reach significance)

Task
One-tailed Hypothesis

title: Chapter 3: Research Design Framework
text:
Part 4: Descriptive Statistics
Before running statistical tests, we need to describe our data. Descriptive statistics summarise the key features.

The Mean
The mean is the arithmetic average — the most common measure of central tendency.
\[\bar{x} = \frac{\sum x_i}{n}\]
Calculating by hand:

Add up all values (Σx)
Divide by the number of values (n)

Example: Memory scores: 5, 7, 6, 8, 9

Sum: 5 + 7 + 6 + 8 + 9 = 35
Count: 5
Mean: 35 ÷ 5 = 7



The Standard Deviation
The mean alone doesn’t tell the whole story. Two groups can have the same mean but look very different:

Group A: 6, 6, 7, 7, 8 (Mean = 6.8)
Group B: 2, 5, 7, 9, 11 (Mean = 6.8)

Group B is much more spread out. We need to measure this variability.

Standard Deviation (SD) measures how spread out the data is from the mean.

Low SD = scores clustered together (consistent)
High SD = scores spread out (variable)




Calculating SD by Hand
Formula:
\[s = \sqrt{\frac{\sum (x_i - \bar{x})^2}{n-1}}\]
Steps:

Calculate the mean
Subtract the mean from each value (deviation)
Square each deviation
Sum the squared deviations
Divide by (n-1)
Take the square root

Example: Scores: 5, 7, 6, 8, 9 (Mean = 7)



Score
Deviation (x - mean)
Squared




5
5 - 7 = -2
4


7
7 - 7 = 0
0


6
6 - 7 = -1
1


8
8 - 7 = +1
1


9
9 - 7 = +2
4


Sum

10




Variance = 10 ÷ (5-1) = 2.5
SD = √2.5 = 1.58



Why n-1?
We divide by (n-1), not n, because we’re estimating the population SD from a sample. This “degrees of freedom” correction makes our estimate unbiased.


Interpreting SD
For normally distributed data:

~68% of values fall within 1 SD of the mean
~95% fall within 2 SDs
~99.7% fall within 3 SDs

If the mean memory score is 7 with SD = 1.58:

About 68% of people scored between 5.4 and 8.6
About 95% scored between 3.8 and 10.2



The Key Insight






ImportantSignal vs Noise



A difference between means only matters if it’s big relative to the spread.

Signal = difference between group means
Noise = variability within groups (SD)
The key question: Is the signal bigger than the noise?

title: Chapter 3: Research Design Framework
text:
Part 5: Reporting Descriptive Statistics
When writing up research, report descriptives clearly using APA format.

Basic Format
Report both mean AND standard deviation:

(M = value, SD = value)

Example:

Participants’ memory scores were moderate (M = 6.8, SD = 1.58).



Comparing Groups
When comparing conditions, report descriptives for each:

Lab A participants (M = 5.8, SD = 1.4) recalled fewer words than Lab B participants (M = 6.5, SD = 1.3).



APA Conventions

Use italics for statistical symbols: M, SD, t, p, r, d
Report two decimal places
No leading zero for values that cannot exceed 1 (e.g., p = .023, not p = 0.023)

title: Week 12 Self-Assessment
text:
Part 1: Reading R Descriptive Output
For the EDS Assignment, you’ll receive R output and need to interpret it. Let’s practice!

Exercise 1: Basic Descriptive Output
A researcher measured the number of words recalled by 8 participants. Here’s the R output:
> summary_stats <- data %>%
+   summarise(
+     Mean = mean(words_recalled),
+     SD = sd(words_recalled),
+     Median = median(words_recalled),
+     n = n()
+   )
> summary_stats

# A tibble: 1 x 4
   Mean    SD Median     n
  <dbl> <dbl>  <dbl> <int>
1   6.5  1.41      6     8
a) What is the mean number of words recalled?






TipShow Answer





The mean is 6.5 words (shown in the Mean column).



b) What is the standard deviation?






TipShow Answer





The standard deviation is 1.41 words (shown in the SD column).



c) What does the comparison of mean (6.5) and median (6) suggest about the distribution?






TipShow Answer





The mean (6.5) is slightly higher than the median (6), suggesting a very slight positive skew. However, they’re close enough that the distribution is approximately symmetric.






Exercise 2: Group Comparison Output
A study compared reaction times between two conditions. Here’s the R output:
> data %>%
+   group_by(condition) %>%
+   summarise(Mean = mean(RT), SD = sd(RT), n = n())

# A tibble: 2 x 4
  condition  Mean    SD     n
  <chr>     <dbl> <dbl> <int>
1 caffeine   285.  42.3    15
2 placebo    312.  51.1    15
a) How many participants were in each condition?






TipShow Answer





15 participants in each condition (shown in the n column).



b) Which condition had faster reaction times?






TipShow Answer





The caffeine condition had faster reaction times (lower mean: 285ms vs 312ms).



c) Write a sentence describing these results in APA format.






TipShow Answer






Participants in the caffeine condition responded faster (M = 285ms, SD = 42.3ms) than those in the placebo condition (M = 312ms, SD = 51.1ms).

title: Week 12 Self-Assessment
text:
Part 2: Interpreting Distributions

Exercise 3: Distribution Shapes
For each scenario, predict the distribution shape:
a) Exam scores on an easy test (most students score 80-100%)






TipShow Answer





Negatively skewed (ceiling effect). Most scores cluster near the top, with a tail toward lower scores.



b) Reaction times to a visual stimulus






TipShow Answer





Positively skewed. There’s a lower bound (can’t be negative or below ~150ms), but no upper bound. Occasional slow responses create a right tail.



c) Heights of adult women






TipShow Answer





Approximately normal (symmetric, bell-shaped). Heights tend to cluster around the average with fewer very short or very tall individuals.





Exercise 4: Mean vs Median in R Output
A researcher reports this R output:
> salary_stats
# A tibble: 1 x 2
     Mean Median
    <dbl>  <dbl>
1  52000  38000
a) What does this tell you about the distribution?






TipShow Answer





The mean (£52,000) is much higher than the median (£38,000), indicating positive skew. A few very high salaries pull the mean up.



b) Which measure (mean or median) better represents the “typical” salary? Why?






TipShow Answer





The median (£38,000) better represents the typical salary because it’s not affected by the extreme high values. More than half of workers earn less than the mean.

title: Week 12 Self-Assessment
section: Part 3: APA Reporting from R Output
text:
Part 3: APA Reporting from R Output

Exercise 5: Complete the Report
Use this R output to answer the questions:
> memory_stats
# A tibble: 1 x 3
   Mean    SD Median
  <dbl> <dbl>  <dbl>
1   6.8   1.4      7
Fill in the blanks:

Participants recalled an average of _____ words (M = _____, SD = _____). The median was _____, suggesting the distribution was approximately _____.







TipShow Answer






Participants recalled an average of 6.8 words (M = 6.8, SD = 1.4). The median was 7, suggesting the distribution was approximately symmetric (since mean ≈ median).






Exercise 6: Write Full APA Description
Use this R output:
> data %>%
+   group_by(time_of_day) %>%
+   summarise(Mean = mean(accuracy), SD = sd(accuracy), n = n())

# A tibble: 2 x 4
  time_of_day  Mean    SD     n
  <chr>       <dbl> <dbl> <int>
1 morning      78.2  12.4    20
2 evening      71.5  14.1    20
Write a complete sentence reporting these descriptives in APA format.






TipShow Answer






Participants showed higher accuracy in the morning (M = 78.2%, SD = 12.4%) compared to the evening (M = 71.5%, SD = 14.1%).

Or:

Mean accuracy was higher in the morning condition (M = 78.2, SD = 12.4) than in the evening condition (M = 71.5, SD = 14.1).

title: Week 12 Self-Assessment
text:
Part 4: Conceptual Questions

Exercise 7: True or False
Mark each statement True or False:
a) The mean is always the best measure of central tendency.






TipShow Answer





False. The median is better for skewed data or when outliers are present.



b) Standard deviation tells you about the shape of the distribution.






TipShow Answer





False. SD tells you about spread/variability, not shape. You need to compare mean and median (or look at a histogram) to assess shape.



c) If the mean is greater than the median, the distribution is positively skewed.






TipShow Answer





True. In a positively skewed distribution, extreme high values pull the mean above the median.



d) In R output, n typically refers to the sample size.






TipShow Answer





True. The n column shows the number of observations (participants/data points) in each group.





Exercise 8: The 68-95-99.7 Rule
Reaction times are normally distributed with Mean = 300ms and SD = 40ms.
a) What range contains approximately 68% of reaction times?






TipShow Answer





Mean ± 1 SD = 300 ± 40 = 260ms to 340ms



b) What range contains approximately 95% of reaction times?






TipShow Answer





Mean ± 2 SD = 300 ± 80 = 220ms to 380ms



c) A participant has a reaction time of 200ms. Is this unusual? Why?






TipShow Answer





Yes, this is unusual. 200ms is (300-200)/40 = 2.5 SDs below the mean. Only about 0.6% of values fall this far from the mean in a normal distribution.

title: Chapter 4: Descriptive Statistics in Action
text:
Part 1: Describing the Centre
When we collect data, the first question is usually: What’s typical?

The Mean: The Balancing Point
The mean is the arithmetic average. If we measured 5 people’s memory scores:

Please enable JavaScript to experience the dynamic code cell content on this page.
The mean is 7. This is the “balancing point” — if you put these scores on a seesaw, 7 is where it would balance.


The Median: The Middle Value
The median is the middle value when data are sorted. Half the values are above it, half below.

Please enable JavaScript to experience the dynamic code cell content on this page.
With 5 values, the median is the 3rd value (when sorted). Here, both mean and median are 7.


When Mean and Median Differ
Sometimes they tell different stories. Consider these scores:

Please enable JavaScript to experience the dynamic code cell content on this page.
The mean shoots up to 10, but the median stays at 7. The median is resistant to extreme values (outliers). The mean is pulled by them.
When to use which?

Mean: When data are roughly symmetric, no extreme outliers
Median: When data are skewed or have outliers (like income data)

title: Chapter 4: Descriptive Statistics in Action
text:
Part 2: Describing the Spread
The centre isn’t the whole story. Two groups can have the same mean but look completely different:

Please enable JavaScript to experience the dynamic code cell content on this page.
Both means are 7, but the groups are very different. We need measures of spread.

The Range: Simplest Spread
The range is just the distance from lowest to highest:

Please enable JavaScript to experience the dynamic code cell content on this page.
Group A spans 2 points (6 to 8). Group B spans 10 points (2 to 12). The range immediately shows Group B is more variable.
Limitation: The range only uses two values, so it’s sensitive to outliers.


The Standard Deviation: The Gold Standard
The standard deviation (SD) measures how far scores typically fall from the mean.

Please enable JavaScript to experience the dynamic code cell content on this page.
Group A’s SD is about 0.7 — scores cluster tightly around 7. Group B’s SD is about 4.2 — scores are much more spread out.
Rule of thumb: In roughly normal data, about 68% of values fall within 1 SD of the mean.
If the mean is 7 and SD is 1:

~68% of scores fall between 6 and 8



The summary() Function: Everything at Once
R’s summary() function gives you a quick overview:

Please enable JavaScript to experience the dynamic code cell content on this page.
This shows:

Min and Max (the range endpoints)
1st and 3rd Quartile (the middle 50%)
Median (the middle value)
Mean

Part 3: Seeing Descriptives in Psychology Data
Let’s look at what descriptive statistics tell us with realistic psychology examples.

Example 1: Reaction Times
Imagine we measured 10 participants’ reaction times (in milliseconds):

Please enable JavaScript to experience the dynamic code cell content on this page.
Interpretation:

Mean reaction time is about 285ms
The median (284ms) is similar, suggesting roughly symmetric data
SD of about 28ms tells us most people fall within ±28ms of the mean

Example 2: Memory Scores by Condition
Now let’s compare two groups. Lab A saw abstract words, Lab B saw concrete words:

Please enable JavaScript to experience the dynamic code cell content on this page.

Lab A mean: ~5.3 words recalled
Lab B mean: ~7.3 words recalled
The difference is 2 words — but is that meaningful?
Both SDs are around 1, so 2 words is about 2 standard deviations — a substantial difference



Example 3: Pre-Post Mood Ratings
Same people rated their mood before and after the session:

Please enable JavaScript to experience the dynamic code cell content on this page.

Mean mood increased by 1.1 points on average

The SD only makes sense relative to the mean and the scale.

RT: Mean = 277ms, SD = 23ms. Is that a lot of variability? It’s about 8% of the mean — fairly typical for reaction times.

Key Concepts

Variables

Independent Variable (IV): What the researcher manipulates or selects
Dependent Variable (DV): What the researcher measures

Design Types

Between-subjects: Different participants in each condition (e.g., Room A vs Room B)

Matched pairs: Participants paired on key characteristics
Correlational: Measuring relationships between variables (no manipulation)



Hypotheses

text:
TipBefore You Begin



This is your first reading for PS50008A. Take your time with it. The concepts introduced here form the foundation for everything else in this module.




You chose psychology because you want to understand people. Why do we remember some things and forget others? What drives someone to help a stranger—or to hurt them? How do our early experiences shape who we become? These questions drew you here, and they’re genuinely worth exploring.
Then you look at your timetable and see “Research Methods and Experimental Design.”
If your heart sinks a little, you’re not alone - but I’m going to try to turn this around. This material has a reputation, and not a glamorous one. But there are real reasons it’s central to your degree—not because we enjoy watching you suffer, but because it changes what you’re capable of doing. It’s powerful stuff!

TipBefore You Begin

You chose psychology because you want to understand people. Why do we remember some things and forget others? What drives someone to help a stranger—or to hurt them? How do our early experiences shape who we become? These questions drew you here, and they’re genuinely worth exploring.
Then you look at your timetable and see “Research Methods and Experimental Design.”
If your heart sinks a little, you’re not alone - but I’m going to try to turn this around. This material has a reputation, and not a glamorous one. But there are real reasons it’s central to your degree—not because we enjoy watching you suffer, but because it changes what you’re capable of doing. It’s powerful stuff!

title: Chapter 1: Introduction to Research Methods
section: 2 You’re Learning to Ask Questions Properly
text:
2 You’re Learning to Ask Questions Properly
Right now, if someone asked you “Does social media cause anxiety?”, you might have an opinion. Everyone has one of those. But psychology isn’t about opinions—it’s about evidence. And evidence doesn’t just land in your lap. Someone has to design a way to gather it, collect it carefully, and work out what it actually shows.
That’s what you’re learning to do. By the end of your degree, you won’t just think social media might cause anxiety—you’ll be able to design a study that could actually test the idea, spot the weaknesses in existing research, and understand why the answer might be more complicated than the headlines suggest.

Think about that for a second… You don’t have to rely on anecdote or opinion anymore. You can create knowledge.

title: Chapter 1: Introduction to Research Methods
text:
3 You’ll See Through the Nonsense
We’re surrounded by claims about human behaviour. Adverts tell us certain products will make us more confident. Influencers promote supplements that supposedly sharpen your mind. News stories announce that scientists have “proved” all sorts of things about personality, intelligence, or relationships. 9 out of 10 adverts are dubious! (not a real stat!)
Most of these claims are, at best, oversimplified. Many are outright wrong. Understanding research methods gives you the ability to look at a study and ask:

How many people did they actually test?
Could something else explain these results?
Is this finding likely to replicate?

This isn’t just academic scepticism. It’s protection against being manipulated by people who use the language of science without the rigour, without the appropriate ‘methods’.

title: Chapter 1: Introduction to Research Methods
text:
4 These Skills Travel
Psychology graduates end up in all sorts of places: clinical training, education, marketing, human resources, policy research, user experience design, data analysis, all sorts of entrepreneurial activities I don’t understand. What connects these fields is that they all involve understanding people and making decisions based on evidence. It’s just thinking scientifically.
The ability to gather data systematically, analyse it honestly, and communicate what it means is valuable almost everywhere. It’s also incredibly rare. Many people can express opinions confidently; fewer can actually interrogate those opinions with evidence.

title: Chapter 1: Introduction to Research Methods
text:
5 And One More Thing
Some of you will genuinely enjoy this. Not everyone, and probably not immediately, but there’s real satisfaction in solving methodological puzzles: working out how to test something that seems untestable, spotting a flaw in an argument, seeing a pattern emerge from data you collected yourself.
I’m not promising you’ll love every moment. But we are promising that this material is worth taking seriously—and that taking it seriously might surprise you.






ImportantThis Week



Since Week 11 has no lecture, use this reading to prepare for the term ahead. But above all, be curious!








Note



Sophie von Stumm (formerly from Goldsmiths!) and colleagues (2011) sought to identify the best predictors of academic performance. Unsurprisingly perhaps, a person’s intelligence was the best predictor. However, they also found that this was matched by the combined predictive power of effort and intellectual curiosity. They conclude that succeeding in academic fields (such as psychology) is not just a question of being smart and trying hard, it is also about having a hungry mind!

Von Stumm, S., Hell, B., & Chamorro-Premuzic, T. (2011). The hungry mind: Intellectual curiosity is the third pillar of academic performance. Perspectives on Psychological Science, 6, 574-588.

title: Chapter 1: Introduction to Research Methods
text:
6 Why Do Psychologists Do Research?
Psychology aims to understand human behaviour and mental processes. But how do we move from casual observation to scientific knowledge?

6.1 The Problem with Common Sense
We often think we understand human behaviour based on everyday experience - my mum certainly thinks so. But “common sense” has limitations (sorry, mum!):

Hindsight bias: Events seem obvious after they occur (“I knew it all along”)
Confirmation bias: We notice evidence that supports our beliefs and ignore contradicting evidence
Anecdotal evidence: Individual cases can mislead — your friend’s experience isn’t representative of everyone

Consider these “common sense” claims:

“Opposites attract” — But also “Birds of a feather flock together”
“Too many cooks spoil the broth” — But also “Many hands make light work”
“Absence makes the heart grow fonder” — But also “Out of sight, out of mind”

Common sense can justify almost any conclusion. Research methods provide systematic tools to overcome these biases and determine which claims actually hold up under scrutiny.


6.2 Why Intuitions About Behaviour Are Often Wrong
Our intuitions fail us for several reasons:

We don’t see our own blind spots — We’re unaware of the biases affecting our judgement
Memory is reconstructive — We misremember events to fit our current beliefs
We overgeneralise from small samples — One or two examples feel like proof
We confuse correlation with causation — Two things happening together doesn’t mean one caused the other

For example, studies consistently show that:

People are poor at predicting what will make them happy
Eyewitness testimony is far less reliable than we assume
“Venting” anger often increases rather than decreases aggression

These findings contradict common intuitions — which is precisely why we need systematic research.

title: Chapter 1: Introduction to Research Methods
text:
7 What Makes a Claim Scientific?

7.1 The Difference Between Opinion and Science
An opinion is a personal belief that may or may not be supported by evidence: > “I think social media makes people unhappy.”
A scientific claim is testable, based on systematic evidence, and open to being proven wrong: > “In a study of 1,000 adults, those who used social media for more than 3 hours daily reported lower life satisfaction scores (M = 5.2) than those who used it less than 1 hour (M = 6.8), t(998) = 4.32, p < .001.”


7.2 Four Hallmarks of Scientific Claims


Empirical basis — Based on observable, measurable evidence, not just reasoning or authority
Systematic collection — Data gathered using consistent, documented methods
Falsifiability — The claim could, in principle, be proven wrong by evidence
Transparency — Methods are described clearly enough that others could repeat them




7.3 What “Replicable” Means
A finding is replicable if other researchers, following the same procedures, get the same results.
Why does this matter?

A single study might have flaws we don’t notice
Random chance can produce misleading results
Researcher bias might influence findings

When multiple independent teams find the same result, we can be more confident it’s real.






NoteThe Replication Crisis



Psychology has faced a “replication crisis” — many classic findings failed to replicate when researchers tried to repeat them. This has led to better practices: larger samples, pre-registration of hypotheses, and more transparency. You’ll learn about this in Week 17.

title: Chapter 1: Introduction to Research Methods
text:
8 The Scientific Method
Researchers typically follow these steps:

8.1 1. Identify a Question
Start with curiosity. What do you want to understand?

“Do people remember information better if they test themselves rather than just re-reading?”



8.2 2. Review Existing Knowledge
What have others already discovered? Build on previous work rather than starting from scratch.


8.3 3. Formulate a Hypothesis
Make a specific, testable prediction.

“Students who use self-testing will recall more information after one week than students who re-read the material.”



8.4 4. Design a Study
Plan exactly how you’ll test your hypothesis: - Who will you study? - What will you measure? - How will you control for other explanations?


8.5 5. Collect Data
Gather observations systematically, following your planned procedures.


8.6 6. Analyse Results
Use statistics to determine whether your findings are meaningful or could have occurred by chance.


8.7 7. Draw Conclusions
What do your results mean? Do they support your hypothesis? What are the limitations?


8.8 8. Report Findings
Share your methods and results so others can evaluate and build on your work.
You’ll work through all these steps in your group project this term.

title: Chapter 1: Introduction to Research Methods
text:
9 Variables: Things That Vary
A variable is anything that can take different values.

9.1 Examples of Variables



Variable
Possible Values




Height
150cm, 165cm, 180cm…


Reaction time
200ms, 350ms, 420ms…


Mood
Happy, sad, anxious, neutral…


Number of words recalled
0, 1, 2, 3… 20


Exam score
0-100





9.2 Why Variables Matter
Research is fundamentally about understanding how variables relate to each other:

Does study time affect exam performance?
Does sleep quality predict reaction time?
Is age related to memory capacity?

In DataLab, you’ll measure several variables and see how they differ between people and across conditions.


9.3 Types of Variables
Continuous variables can take any value within a range: - Height (175.3cm) - Reaction time (287.4ms) - Temperature (36.8°C)
Categorical variables fall into distinct categories: - Gender (male, female, non-binary) - Experimental condition (control, treatment) - Handedness (left, right, ambidextrous)
Discrete variables are countable whole numbers: - Number of items recalled (7) - Number of errors (3) - Number of children (2)
Understanding variable types helps you choose appropriate statistical analyses — something you’ll learn throughout this module.

title: Chapter 1: Introduction to Research Methods
section: 10 How Empirical Evidence Helps Us Understand Behaviour
text:
10 How Empirical Evidence Helps Us Understand Behaviour

10.1 Moving Beyond Speculation
Without data, debates about human behaviour often go in circles. Everyone has opinions, but how do we know whose is correct?
Empirical evidence allows us to:

Test competing theories — Instead of arguing, we can design studies to see which prediction holds
Discover unexpected findings — Data often reveals patterns we wouldn’t have predicted
Quantify effects — Not just “X affects Y” but “X increases Y by approximately this much”
Identify boundary conditions — Under what circumstances does a finding hold or not hold?



10.2 An Example: Does Punishment Deter Crime?
Common sense might suggest that harsher punishments reduce crime. But what does the evidence show?
Research has found: - Certainty of punishment matters more than severity - Very harsh sentences may actually increase recidivism in some cases - Deterrent effects vary by crime type and offender characteristics
Without systematic data collection, we’d have no way to discover these nuances.

title: Chapter 1: Introduction to Research Methods
text:
11 Connecting to DataLab

11.1 Your Data, Your Learning
In Thursday’s lab, you’ll experience research from both perspectives:

As a participant — completing cognitive tasks
As a tester — administering tasks and recording data

This dual perspective helps you understand:

Why standardised procedures matter (you’ll see what happens when instructions vary)
How measurement introduces variability (the same person gives different responses across trials)
What it feels like to generate data that will be analysed

The data you generate will be used throughout the term. When we discuss distributions in Week 12, we’ll look at the distribution of YOUR reaction times. When we learn about t-tests in Week 14, we’ll compare performance between Room A and Room B. This is your data, and you’ll learn statistics by exploring it.

title: Chapter 3: Research Design Framework
text:
TipBefore You Begin



This is the most important reading of the term. It introduces ALL the terminology you need for your Research Plan. Take your time — everything connects.


This reading covers:

Independent and dependent variables

title: Chapter 3: Research Design Framework
text:
2 Part 1: The Building Blocks — Variables

2.1 What Is a Variable?
A variable is anything that can vary — any characteristic, number, or quantity that can take different values.
In the DataLab:

Memory scores varied (some people remembered 4 words, others 8)
Mood ratings varied (some felt 3/10, others 8/10)
Reaction times varied (some caught the ruler quickly, others slowly)



2.2 Independent and Dependent Variables
In experimental research, we distinguish between two types of variables:

Independent Variable (IV): What the researcher manipulates or controls — the presumed cause.
Dependent Variable (DV): What the researcher measures — the outcome that may be affected.

The DV depends on the IV. We’re asking: Does the outcome depend on the condition?


2.3 DataLab Example: Memory Task
In the memory experiment:

IV: Word type (abstract vs concrete)
DV: Number of words recalled (0-10)

Lab A saw abstract words (justice, freedom, wisdom). Lab B saw concrete words (chair, river, mountain). The researcher manipulated which words you saw — that’s the IV.
What we measured — how many words you recalled — is the DV. We wanted to know if recall depended on the word type.


2.4 When There Is No IV
Not all research involves manipulation. Sometimes we simply measure two things and look at their relationship.
In the Frontal Lob task, you rated how good you thought you’d be at throwing (1-10), and then we measured your actual accuracy. Neither was manipulated — we just measured both.






ImportantKey Insight



When there’s no manipulation, there’s no IV. This is called a correlational design, and we’ll cover it shortly.




2.5 Data Types
The DV can be measured in different ways:








Data Type
Description
Example




Continuous
Can take any value (including decimals)
Reaction time (245.3ms)


Discrete
Whole numbers only (counts)
Words recalled (7)


Categorical
Categories with no numerical order
Lab group (A or B)


Ordinal
Categories with an order
Rating (1-10 scale)



In the DataLab:

Memory score is discrete (you can’t recall 6.5 words)
Reaction time is continuous (could be 245.3ms or 245.4ms)
Mood rating is ordinal (1-10 scale with order, but intervals may not be equal)

title: Chapter 3: Research Design Framework
text:
3 Part 2: Design Types
The design refers to how participants are assigned to conditions.

3.1 Between-Subjects Design

Between-subjects design: Different participants in each condition.

In the memory experiment, you were in either Lab A (abstract words) or Lab B (concrete words) — never both. Different people were in each condition.
Why “between”? We’re comparing between groups — Lab A people versus Lab B people.
Advantage: No order effects (practice, fatigue, boredom)
Disadvantage: Individual differences may affect results (maybe Lab B just happened to have better memorisers)


3.2 Within-Subjects Design

Within-subjects design: The same participants measured in all conditions.

In the pre-post mood survey, you rated your mood before and after the session. The same person provided both data points.
Why “within”? We’re comparing within the same person — your pre-mood versus your post-mood.
Advantage: Each person is their own control! Individual differences are controlled because we’re comparing you to yourself.
Disadvantage: Order effects possible (practice, fatigue)


3.3 Within-Subjects Examples from DataLab



Task
Same Person Compared




Pre/Post mood
Before vs after session


Pre/Post energy
Before vs after session


Pre/Post stress
Before vs after session


Frontal Lob
Dominant vs non-dominant hand





3.4 Matched Pairs Design

Matched pairs design: Participants are paired on a key characteristic, then one from each pair goes to each condition.

This is a hybrid — different people in each condition (like between-subjects), but they’re matched to be similar (reducing individual difference problems).
Example: Match students by the amount of sleep they reported the night before. Let’s say two participants reported five hours and two participants reported 10 hours. One from each pair gets abstract words, the other gets concrete words. This would allow me to control for sleep quantity (five or ten hours), as I would have each level represented in each group. It means I would have to ask about sleep before allocating to condition, and so is a little bit more complicated in everyday life.


3.5 Correlational Design

Correlational design: Measuring the relationship between two variables — no manipulation.

When we measured self-rating and actual throwing performance, we didn’t manipulate either. We simply measured both and asked: Are they related? This could be the same for hours of sleep and memory performance, or any of the personality traits we measured and any other outcome variable.






WarningCritical Point



In correlational designs, there is NO IV. Neither variable is the “cause” — we’re just measuring a relationship.




3.6 Summary: Design Types








Design
Key Feature
Example




Between-subjects
Different people in each condition
Lab A vs Lab B


Within-subjects
Same people in all conditions
Pre vs Post mood


Matched pairs
Participants paired, one per condition
Matched by ability


Correlational
Relationship measured, no manipulation
Self-rating vs performance

title: Chapter 3: Research Design Framework
text:
4 Part 3: Writing Hypotheses
A hypothesis is a prediction about what you expect to find.

4.1 Experimental vs Null Hypothesis

Experimental hypothesis (H₁ or Ha): Predicts an effect or difference will exist.
Null hypothesis (H₀): Predicts no effect or no difference.

For the memory experiment:

H₁: Concrete words will be easier to remember than abstract words.
H₀: There will be no difference in recall between word types.

Statistical testing works by assuming H₀ is true, then checking if the data is surprising enough to reject that assumption.


4.2 One-Tailed vs Two-Tailed

One-tailed hypothesis: Predicts the direction of the effect.
Two-tailed hypothesis: Predicts a difference but not which direction.

One-tailed examples:

“Concrete words will be easier to remember than abstract words” (predicts concrete > abstract)
“Mood will improve after the session” (predicts post > pre)
“Dominant hand will be more accurate than non-dominant hand” (predicts dominant > non-dominant)

Two-tailed examples:

“Word type will affect memory” (could be better or worse)
“Mood will change after the session” (could go up or down)
“There will be a difference in accuracy between hands” (no direction predicted)



4.3 When to Use Which?
Use one-tailed when:

Previous research strongly suggests a direction
Your theory predicts a specific direction
You only care about effects in one direction

Use two-tailed when:

You’re uncertain about the direction
Effects in either direction would be interesting
You’re being conservative (harder to reach significance)



4.4 Hypotheses for Each DataLab Task



Task
One-tailed Hypothesis




Memory
Concrete words will be recalled better than abstract words


Pre-Post Mood
Mood will improve after the session


Frontal Lob
Dominant hand will be more accurate than non-dominant


Sixth Sense
Detection accuracy will be greater than chance (50%)

title: Chapter 3: Research Design Framework
text:
5 Part 4: Descriptive Statistics
Before running statistical tests, we need to describe our data. Descriptive statistics summarise the key features.

5.1 The Mean
The mean is the arithmetic average — the most common measure of central tendency.
\[\bar{x} = \frac{\sum x_i}{n}\]
Calculating by hand:

Add up all values (Σx)
Divide by the number of values (n)

Example: Memory scores: 5, 7, 6, 8, 9

Sum: 5 + 7 + 6 + 8 + 9 = 35
Count: 5
Mean: 35 ÷ 5 = 7



5.2 The Standard Deviation
The mean alone doesn’t tell the whole story. Two groups can have the same mean but look very different:

Group A: 6, 6, 7, 7, 8 (Mean = 6.8)
Group B: 2, 5, 7, 9, 11 (Mean = 6.8)

Group B is much more spread out. We need to measure this variability.

Standard Deviation (SD) measures how spread out the data is from the mean.

Low SD = scores clustered together (consistent)
High SD = scores spread out (variable)




5.3 Calculating SD by Hand
Formula:
\[s = \sqrt{\frac{\sum (x_i - \bar{x})^2}{n-1}}\]
Steps:

Calculate the mean
Subtract the mean from each value (deviation)
Square each deviation
Sum the squared deviations
Divide by (n-1)
Take the square root

Example: Scores: 5, 7, 6, 8, 9 (Mean = 7)



Score
Deviation (x - mean)
Squared




5
5 - 7 = -2
4


7
7 - 7 = 0
0


6
6 - 7 = -1
1


8
8 - 7 = +1
1


9
9 - 7 = +2
4


Sum

10




Variance = 10 ÷ (5-1) = 2.5
SD = √2.5 = 1.58



5.4 Why n-1?
We divide by (n-1), not n, because we’re estimating the population SD from a sample. This “degrees of freedom” correction makes our estimate unbiased.


5.5 Interpreting SD
For normally distributed data:

~68% of values fall within 1 SD of the mean
~95% fall within 2 SDs
~99.7% fall within 3 SDs

If the mean memory score is 7 with SD = 1.58:

About 68% of people scored between 5.4 and 8.6
About 95% scored between 3.8 and 10.2



5.6 The Key Insight






ImportantSignal vs Noise



A difference between means only matters if it’s big relative to the spread.

Signal = difference between group means
Noise = variability within groups (SD)
The key question: Is the signal bigger than the noise?

title: Chapter 3: Research Design Framework
text:
6 Part 5: Reporting Descriptive Statistics
When writing up research, report descriptives clearly using APA format.

6.1 Basic Format
Report both mean AND standard deviation:

(M = value, SD = value)

Example:

Participants’ memory scores were moderate (M = 6.8, SD = 1.58).



6.2 Comparing Groups
When comparing conditions, report descriptives for each:

Lab A participants (M = 5.8, SD = 1.4) recalled fewer words than Lab B participants (M = 6.5, SD = 1.3).



6.3 APA Conventions

Use italics for statistical symbols: M, SD, t, p, r, d
Report two decimal places
No leading zero for values that cannot exceed 1 (e.g., p = .023, not p = 0.023)

2 Conceptual Questions

2.1 Question 1: Why Research Methods?
Why is “common sense” unreliable for understanding human behaviour?
It’s always wrongIt suffers from biases like hindsight and confirmation biasScientists don’t like common senseIt only works for simple behaviours


Show explanation

Common sense is unreliable because of:

Hindsight bias — events seem obvious after they occur
Confirmation bias — we notice supporting evidence and ignore contradicting evidence
Anecdotal evidence — individual cases can mislead
Common sense can justify contradictory conclusions (e.g., “opposites attract” vs “birds of a feather flock together”)
